  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper restates that using amplitude estimation within QAMC yields a sampling error scaling of order 1/NQ, leading to a quadratic improvement over classical Monte Carlo, and notes that the overall QAMC algorithm is quadratically better in cost terms; they show that a naïve square-root encoding fails to converge for negative payoffs, while the proposed combination of direct encoding and mRQAE can recover the true (negative) price without extra mechanisms and exhibits reasonable performance on positive-payoff contracts, with mRQAE claimed to be asymptotically more efficient and the overall new methodology described as competitive in terms of speed with current standards.

On the hardware side, the authors stress that practical implementation is constrained by state-of-the-art devices: the oracle implementation requires an excessively large number of qubits, Grover-like routine depths are not feasible given current decoherence times, and the total gate count implies gate error requirements beyond current technology. They also remark that, overall, many issues remain to be solved in practice when current hardware constraints are considered.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-016, C-022, C-024, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]

    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-031, C-032]

=== PAPER 3f4c5ad6749d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets quantum pricing of a single-asset European-style option, motivated by the cost of classical Monte Carlo simulations for estimating expected option returns. It formulates the problem as preparing the probability distribution of the asset price at maturity on a quantum register and then computing the expected payoff within this representation, with a focus on designing an efficient way to load this distribution as a prerequisite for quantum speedups over Monte Carlo.
    [codes: C-001, C-010, C-012, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a three-part quantum option-pricing algorithm using a unary encoding where exactly one qubit in the register is in state |1⟩ per basis element: (1) a low-depth amplitude loading circuit that prepares the asset-price distribution at maturity using partial-SWAP gates whose angles encode time dependence, (2) a payoff computation step implemented with simple controlled-Ry gates that map the payoff into the probability of measuring an ancilla qubit, and (3) a standard amplitude estimation stage with a simplified oracle and reflection operator S0 constructed from only a few gates. The unary layout assumes qubits arranged on a 1D line with two-local interactions and can benefit from hardware that natively supports partial-iSWAP-like interactions.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-014, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-004, C-022, C-023, C-005, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The unary representation is reported to substantially simplify circuit structure, yielding low and time-independent depth for distribution loading (⌊n/2⌋+1) and overall O(n) partial-SWAP and O(κn) controlled-Ry gates, as well as a simplified S0 operator in amplitude estimation. In noisy simulations with depolarizing and readout errors, the unary scheme achieves about an order-of-magnitude lower KL divergence than the binary algorithm for the same tolerated error in distribution loading, and shows smaller deviation from the mean payoff estimate, with amplitude estimation reducing payoff uncertainty over iterations. The authors also observe that with around 50 bins, classical discretization errors in the option price can already be brought below about 0.5%, suggesting that moderate bin counts suffice for accurate pricing, and they find that the unary algorithm is more robust to low noise levels than the binary counterpart for several AE iterations.
    [codes: C-006, C-016, C-019, C-025, C-030, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum approach is positioned against classical Monte Carlo, which is characterized as computationally costly for estimating expected option returns, and the use of amplitude estimation is said to offer a quadratic reduction in the number of required quantum circuit runs compared to classical Monte Carlo samples, conditional on efficient distribution loading. Additionally, the study compares unary and binary quantum encodings rather than directly to classical methods, using error maps and KL divergence, and notes that with roughly 50 bins classical discretization error in option prices can already be below 0.5%, providing a classical accuracy reference point.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge that unary encoding incurs linear qubit overhead, requiring linearly many qubits in the number of bins and offering lower precision than binary encoding for a fixed qubit budget. They note that readout on all qubits is necessary to enable the post-selection error-mitigation scheme, and that post-selection itself discards an increasing fraction of shots as the number of bins grows, which can erode the effective sampling rate and must be controlled to preserve any quantum advantage. The approach further depends on having an efficient way to load the asset-price probability distribution; without such state preparation, the quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation cannot be realized. On the simulation side, they use a depolarizing-noise model and explicitly neglect thermal relaxation and dephasing, justifying this by the shallow circuit depths and short execution times relative to coherence times, but this is presented as a modelling simplification. They also indicate that the binary approach demands non-local chip connectivity, which is a practical hardware limitation for that baseline rather than for unary itself.
    [codes: C-008, C-012, C-015, C-026, C-034, C-035, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-029]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper frames the unary algorithm as targeting an intermediate regime between today’s devices and fully fault-tolerant quantum computers and suggests several extensions, including adapting the encoding so qubits represent non-equispaced bins to increase precision and exploring extensions to multi-asset option computations. These are mentioned as available ideas rather than fully developed methods.
    [codes: C-046, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The main contribution is presented as a quantum option-pricing algorithm based on unary encoding of the asset price, which, according to the authors, allows for low-depth, structurally simple circuits with 1D nearest-neighbor connectivity and built-in post-selection for error mitigation, in contrast to binary encodings that require fewer qubits but deeper, more connectivity-demanding circuits and more complex oracles. They further claim that, despite the linear qubit cost, unary representation may offer a practically relevant advantage on near-term devices, particularly for a modest number of bins (on the order of up to ~100) and on hardware with native partial-iSWAP interactions where amplitude distribution can be implemented with substantially fewer gates.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-009, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors base their evaluation on simulated experiments under a depolarizing noise model with specified single- and two-qubit gate and readout error rates, intentionally omitting thermal relaxation and dephasing on the grounds of shallow circuit depth and short execution times. They emphasize that post-selection to enforce consistency with the unary subspace requires full-qubit readout and is central to their error-mitigation strategy, which, combined with fewer gates, is cited as the reason for unary’s improved robustness in noisy simulations. The comparative study with the binary algorithm uses error maps, KL divergence, and payoff deviations, and the paper also notes a specific hardware abstraction (1D nearest-neighbor connectivity and potential native partial-iSWAP gates) as part of its practical evaluation context.
    [codes: C-017, C-018, C-019, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-042]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper remarks that increasing the number of bins tends to increase both the error and uncertainty in the payoff estimate because more instances must be discarded by post-selection, and stresses that any quantum advantage hinges on retaining a sufficient fraction of shots after post-selection, linking algorithmic performance closely to experimental shot efficiency.
    [codes: C-043, C-044, C-045]

    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-018, C-020, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-031]

The authors design and analyze state‑preparation circuits for discrete Markov chains (including two‑state and multi‑state cases), using RY/CRY rotations parameterized by transition probabilities (estimated from NBER business cycle data), and study one‑hot versus binary encodings that trade qubit count against gate complexity. These Markov‑controlled circuits are then embedded into application‑specific architectures: a static credit‑risk state‑preparation circuit with regime‑dependent default probabilities; an option‑pricing circuit with Brownian, price, and payoff registers plus regime‑controlled price updates; and a dynamic portfolio circuit combining a Markov chain, a QFT‑based growth register, and rescaled loss encoding, with MLAE adopted as a near‑term alternative to canonical QAE.

  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On real hardware (IBM torino and Honeywell H1), the authors show that their Markov‑chain state‑preparation circuits achieve low mean squared error (MSE), with accuracy improving for larger transition probabilities and error growth mainly driven by the exponential increase in bins and reduced effective shots. For the static regime‑dependent credit‑risk application and regime‑switching derivative pricing, they report MSE tables for specific parameter choices and observe that one‑hot encoding is preferable up to moderate state counts on current IBM hardware. === PAPER 41a852fada38 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the challenge of representing and analyzing continuous-time stochastic processes (CTSPs) on quantum computers for applications in option pricing and insurance, where analytic solutions for stochastic differential equations are often unavailable and classical numerical methods like Monte Carlo can be computationally demanding. The authors specifically identify two unresolved challenges: efficient quantum state preparation for CTSPs and quantum methods for extracting expectations of weighted path integrals and history-sensitive quantities such as first-hitting times, which are central to quantitative finance and actuarial applications. They instantiate the problem in financial contexts including option pricing under the Merton Jump Diffusion model and ruin probability in the Collective Risk Model, and also highlight the need to extract path-dependent information based on whole trajectory histories.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-034, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a two-stage quantum framework for CTSPs consisting of a data preparation (state preparation) procedure and an information extraction procedure. They introduce two quantum representations for continuous-time stochastic processes (QCTSPs), with associated state preparation methods that reduce qubit counts, improve flexibility, and increase sensitivity to discontinuous jumps; these methods exploit an observation about holding times to design circuits with reduced depth and gate complexity and achieve exponential resource reductions in a key parameter called the average holding time τ_avg. The information extraction stage extends quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo to continuous time by evaluating weightless and time-weighted integrals via Riemann-like decompositions and "directed areas" and by adding sequences of flag qubits to extract history-sensitive quantities such as first-hitting times and path-dependent payoffs, yielding a Monte Carlo-style quantum algorithm with quadratic acceleration. The framework is designed so that the data preparation can also serve as a reusable submodule to alleviate input bottlenecks in other quantum algorithms, and its resource requirements are characterized in terms of time horizon T and process memory length, with specific preparation circuits and scaling bounds derived for several process families (e.g., memory-less exponential holding times, Lévy, Poisson, compound Poisson, continuous Markov, and Cox processes).
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The key technical result is that the proposed data preparation achieves exponential reductions in both space and time complexity with respect to a crucial CTSP feature parameter, concretely instantiated as an exponential reduction in the number of state-space copies from O(T)=O(n·τ_avg) under uniform sampling to O(n·ln τ_avg) under their QCTSP method. For memory-less holding times, they show that the holding time τ_j, which is exponentially distributed, can be prepared using ⌈log(−1/(λ_j ln ε))⌉ qubits with constant circuit depth, and more broadly they claim efficient preparation schemes for Lévy, Poisson, compound Poisson, continuous Markov, and Cox processes, with explicit qubit and circuit-depth scalings provided for each. On the extraction side, they claim a quadratic acceleration over classical Monte Carlo for continuous-time simulations by decoding compressed information via their extended quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo, including efficient evaluation of weightless and time-weighted path integrals and history-sensitive quantities via flag qubits. Application results indicate that their quantum CTSP simulation for option pricing under the Merton Jump Diffusion model is consistent with a 40-term truncated Merton formula and with classical Monte Carlo, and they further connect ruin probability in the Collective Risk Model to their general discounted-penalty framework as a special case.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-037, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors position their method as addressing the high storage and computation demands of classical Monte Carlo for CTSPs by compressing process information and then performing quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo with a quadratic speedup in sample complexity or runtime relative to classical Monte Carlo. They explicitly compare their QCTSP-based simulation for Merton Jump Diffusion option pricing against both a truncated analytic Merton formula and classical Monte Carlo, reporting consistent results, and they contrast their QCTSP resource requirements with those of a classical uniform time-sampling scheme, claiming an exponential reduction in the number of state-space copies. More generally, they describe their approach as an extension of quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo to the continuous-time setting and as a potential subroutine to mitigate classical-like data input bottlenecks in other quantum algorithms.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-006, C-010, C-030, C-031, C-037]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that prior work has not fully resolved the CTSP state preparation problem or the design of quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo methods capable of handling expectations of weighted integrals and history-sensitive information such as first-hitting times, motivating their contributions but also indicating that the broader problem space remains only partially addressed. They further observe that state preparation complexity grows with the memory length of the process, implying that processes with long memory may be harder to treat with their framework. In their conclusion they explicitly state that they have not explored preparation techniques for several other financially relevant CTSPs, including Hawkes processes, flagging these unaddressed process classes as a limitation of the current work.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-020, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work identified by the authors includes extending their preparation techniques to additional continuous-time stochastic processes of financial relevance, such as Hawkes processes, and more broadly exploring CTSP families with richer memory structures where preparation complexity is higher. Implicitly, the unresolved aspects of quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo for complex history-sensitive functionals suggest further research on more general extraction schemes and on scaling their framework to a wider class of path-dependent financial products and insurance contracts.
    [codes: C-013, C-020, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims to introduce an algorithmic quantum framework for continuous-time stochastic processes that integrates compressed data preparation with an extended quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo information extraction stage, offering exponential reductions in key resource parameters and a quadratic acceleration for continuous-time Monte Carlo relative to classical methods. Novel aspects include two general QCTSP encoding schemes with preparation circuits tailored to holding-time structures, enabling exponential resource savings and sensitivity to discontinuous jumps, and a flag-qubit-based method for extracting history-sensitive path information such as first-hitting times, which the authors emphasize as essential for path-dependent option pricing and actuarial computations. They also highlight the breadth of application across statistics, physics, time-series analysis, and finance, with financial and actuarial case studies—Merton Jump Diffusion option pricing and ruin probability in the Collective Risk Model—framing their contribution as introducing quantum computation into aspects of insurance mathematics.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is primarily theoretical and algorithmic, providing resource bounds and circuit constructions for QCTSP preparation and extraction but reporting results via analysis and simulations rather than hardware experiments. They validate their Merton Jump Diffusion option pricing example by comparing QCTSP-based simulations against a truncated analytic formula and classical Monte Carlo, indicating consistency but without detailing datasets or empirical error distributions in the provided excerpts.   DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as solving general time-dependent PDEs via a variational principle and then instantiates this for financial derivative pricing, specifically the multi-asset Black–Scholes PDE for European options on many correlated assets, motivated by overcoming the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional settings where fine-grained state information is required.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-033, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a quantum-inspired variational Monte Carlo framework closely related to VQAs, parameterizing the PDE solution as a positive, normalized neural-network quantum state with an autoregressive factorization and sampling from |ψβ(x)|² for importance sampling, on a meshed spatial grid that is digitized into an n‑qubit state; evolution proceeds via stochastic estimation of overlaps under a time-dependent variational principle, with pretraining to match initial conditions and SVD-regularized linear solves.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-009, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-032, C-034]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For diffusion (heat equation) benchmarks, the variational method produces solutions that match the forward Euler baseline well, though discrepancies grow with spatial dimension; larger Monte Carlo batch sizes substantially reduce relative error. Runtime analysis shows the overall method scaling polynomially with problem size but dominated by the autoregressive sampling cost. Qualitative visualizations indicate that the scheme respects periodic boundary conditions. In Black–Scholes option-pricing experiments, the algorithm is applied across various one- and two-dimensional option types and parameter settings and is reported to achieve satisfactory and robust performance, with particular value claimed in higher-dimensional cases where classical schemes struggle.
    [codes: C-021, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038]

They also emphasize that their formalism parallels finite elements, but classical finite-element methods suffer an exponential problem-size scaling with dimension that their variational approach aims to avoid.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-032, C-034, C-036, C-038]

They acknowledge numerical issues in the evolution step: the matrix M is usually ill-conditioned, requiring SVD-based regularization, and the polynomial-time scaling is obtained at the cost of approximate time evolution due to Monte Carlo estimation. They highlight that classical finite-element approaches suffer from an exponential scaling in dimension, which is part of their motivation but also a point of comparison, and in the financial context they stress that all numerical algorithms including theirs require artificial truncation of the spatial domain, introducing a modeling caveat. They also empirically observe that errors grow with the dimensionality of the problem, indicating degradation in accuracy for higher-dimensional PDEs.

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses derivative pricing and credit risk measurement in financial markets by proposing regime-switching models that are both more realistic and more compatible with near-term quantum hardware. It replaces continuous-time diffusion models, which are viewed as currently impractical for quantum advantage, with discrete-time, discrete-state Markov-chain regime-switching processes whose states represent good and bad economic conditions, and uses these to frame option pricing, portfolio loss distributions, and VaR calculations for quantum algorithms.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-014, C-024, C-032]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors work on gate-based quantum computers, encoding observable two-state Markov chains and associated financial quantities using discrete-time circuits whose depth scales with the number of periods. They exploit exact discrete transition densities of the regime-switching processes to build relatively simple state-preparation circuits, initialize Markov-chain qubits in the steady-state distribution, and construct application-specific operators for credit risk and derivative pricing, including regime-dependent state preparation, Taylor-approximated default-angle mappings, and multi-controlled additions for regime-dependent payoffs. Across applications, they rely on amplitude estimation (canonical and iterative QAE/IQAE) to estimate probabilities or expectations, with additional hybrid structure such as classical preprocessing to reduce qubit counts and a dynamic-portfolio circuit that combines a Markov-chain register with a QFT-based growth register.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For the Markov-chain circuits, the authors report that estimated state probabilities are quite accurate, with MSE behavior driven mainly by the growth of histogram bins and finite shots, and they note that a synthetic high-transition case yields lower MSE due to a wider distribution and error cancellation. In the static credit-risk application, they provide MSE results for portfolio loss computations under different regime specifications, while for derivative pricing they report MSEs for European options under regime switching using specified sampling parameters. They also conclude that, among the financial applications considered, the credit-risk circuit appears to be the more promising candidate for obtaining usable amplitude-estimation-based results on NISQ processors. They emphasize that quantum amplitude estimation is expected to provide quadratic scaling improvements in estimation error over classical Monte Carlo, and note that classical preprocessing (e.g., in the Markowitz portfolio and parameter mappings) is used to control quantum resource requirements.
    [codes: C-010, C-021, C-034, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that current quantum computers are not yet capable of delivering computational advantages for the continuous-time stochastic diffusion models typically used in finance, motivating the shift to discrete regime-switching models. As a modeling simplification, the authors assume that Markov-chain states are ex post observable in the credit-risk setting, explicitly noting this as a convenience. They identify a trade-off in the derivative-pricing post-processing where choosing a smaller payoff-scaling constant reduces approximation error but increases sampling error. At the hardware level, they state that the practical example circuit is prohibitively large for canonical QAE on current processors, that connectivity constraints approximately double the complexity of the transpiled circuits, and that NISQ-era limitations such as the need for error mitigation and tight qubit budgets remain significant obstacles.
    [codes: C-001, C-018, C-031, C-039, C-043, C-045]

    [codes: C-044]

Within this framework, they extend existing credit-risk and derivative-pricing schemes to include regime dependence, develop tailored quantum circuits (including modified state-preparation, loss and payoff operators), and argue that their credit-risk constructions in particular form attractive candidates for NISQ-era amplitude-estimation applications and a broader roadmap for future quantum-finance work.

=== PAPER 49dc03e35036 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies quantum algorithms for pricing complex, path-dependent derivatives—specifically basket autocallables and TARFs—where classical Monte Carlo is computationally expensive due to large path counts and path dependence of payoffs. The authors explicitly focus on derivative types that are ‘complicated enough’ to require large Monte Carlo samples and note that path-dependent structures like autocallables make pricing harder than for plain-vanilla options.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-008, C-020]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is based on amplitude-estimation–style quantum Monte Carlo, leveraging the known quadratic 1/M speedup in Monte Carlo sampling, and is tailored to derivative pricing under geometric Brownian motion. A key methodological contribution is the re-parameterization method, which loads independent standard Gaussian variables in return space via a reusable variationally trained Gaussian loader, then applies affine transformations to generate the required correlated distributions; this avoids the normalization and scaling problems of earlier Grover–Rudolph and Riemann-sum loading schemes and exploits the relative ease of loading return-space normals whose evolution is independent of previous prices.
    [codes: C-003, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors provide what they describe as the first complete resource estimates for useful quantum derivative pricing on realistic benchmarks, finding that their autocallable and TARF cases require around 8k–11.5k logical qubits and T-depths on the order of 5.4×10^7–8.2×10^7, with overall quantum advantage necessitating execution in about a second of logical time. They show that the re-parameterization method significantly reduces computational requirements compared to Riemann-sum loading by avoiding normalization overhead, derive explicit bounds for arithmetic error in terms of Gaussian-loader and payoff errors, and empirically characterize the variational Gaussian loader: energy-based pretraining leads to smoother landscapes than direct L∞ optimization, digitization errors scale as O(1/M_digit), and loader error decays exponentially with circuit size. They also give explicit resource counts for payoff circuits alone (e.g., 1.6k qubits and T-depth 3.2k for autocallables; 9k qubits and T-depth 6k for TARFs) and detailed re-parameterization resource estimates for each benchmark derivative.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-029]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum algorithms are framed as leveraging the quadratic improvement in Monte Carlo sampling complexity via amplitude estimation relative to classical Monte Carlo, with the resource thresholds calibrated so that the total quantum error matches a practically relevant pricing tolerance. The choice to focus on derivatives that demand large Monte Carlo sample sizes is explicitly motivated by the need for instances where classical methods are sufficiently expensive for a quadratic speedup to be valuable.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-001]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several significant limitations. On the algorithmic side, the authors find that existing state-loading methods are problematic: Grover–Rudolph loading is declared insufficient to achieve quantum advantage in derivative pricing, and Riemann-sum–based loading requires restrictive normalization assumptions to prevent errors that grow exponentially in the number of time steps. Even with the improved re-parameterization method, TARF pricing is more error-sensitive because discounting and aggregation across time cause payoff errors to add in quadrature, forcing a stricter per-step error budget. On the hardware side, they note that current estimates for logical clock rates (~10 kHz) are orders of magnitude slower than the roughly one-second execution time required to realize advantage at their resource thresholds, indicating that contemporary hardware is far from meeting the necessary performance.
    [codes: C-009, C-023, C-024, C-027]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors point to several avenues for future improvement and extension. They note that any reduction in the algorithm’s T-depth would linearly relax the stringent logical clock-rate requirement, making advantage easier to reach. They also suggest that their re-parameterization framework, though analyzed under geometric Brownian motion, can be extended straightforwardly to other stochastic models. Additionally, they indicate that importance sampling techniques might mitigate the scaling overhead associated with normalization in Riemann-sum–based loading, potentially making that approach more practical.
    [codes: C-025, C-026, C-028]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims two main contributions: first, it presents the first complete end-to-end resource estimates for achieving useful quantum advantage in derivative pricing on realistic, path-dependent instruments such as autocallables and TARFs; second, it introduces the re-parameterization method for quantum derivative pricing, which uses reusable variationally trained Gaussian loaders in return space to eliminate problematic normalization overhead and reduce computational requirements relative to prior loading methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-012, C-015]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work provides an explicit error-budgeting framework for the re-parameterization approach by decomposing total error into components (e.g., loader, arithmetic, payoff) and deriving analytic bounds for arithmetic error in terms of underlying density and payoff approximation errors. The paper also documents empirical behavior of variational Gaussian loaders, including the benefit of energy-based pretraining over direct L∞ optimization for smoother optimization landscapes, systematic O(1/M_digit) scaling of digitization error, and approximate exponential error decay with increased circuit resources; these observations support the practicality of using a pre-trained, problem-independent Gaussian loader as a reusable subroutine in resource estimates.
    [codes: C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-029]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also emphasizes structural aspects of the financial instruments studied: path-dependent derivatives like autocallables are highlighted as substantially more challenging to price than simpler products, and the authors stress that focusing on such computationally demanding contracts is crucial to identifying realistic settings where quantum Monte Carlo speedups could translate into economically meaningful advantage.
    [codes: C-006, C-008, C-020]

=== PAPER 4c50b01d13fe (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum state preparation as a distribution-generation task, where measurement probabilities must match a desired target distribution for use in simulations and pricing problems. === PAPER 4ceae3900931 (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the problem of pricing multi-asset derivatives by solving the Black–Scholes partial differential equation (BSPDE) on a discretized grid and extracting the option price as an inner product between the PDE solution and a probability distribution, with particular focus on a double knock-out barrier option as a numerical test case. The authors emphasize that classical finite difference methods (FDM) for this BSPDE suffer from time and space complexity that grows exponentially with the number of assets and the desired precision.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-021, C-026]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a variational quantum simulation (VQS) approach to solve the discretized Black–Scholes PDE, embedding the probability distribution of underlying asset prices into quantum amplitudes and then evolving the state under VQS to obtain the derivative-price function. Their algorithm has three main parts: (1) prepare a quantum state encoding the probability distribution, e.g., via VQS for the Fokker–Planck equation or quantum generative models; (2) solve the BSPDE with boundary conditions using VQS; and (3) compute the price as an inner product between the evolved solution state and the probability state using a SWAP test. Implementation-wise, they use amplitude encoding on a grid whose size scales as O((1/ε)^{d/2}), an ansatz-based VQS framework introduced as a method for linear ODEs, Euler integration for parameter evolution, and a SWAP-test circuit to estimate the overlap between price and probability states.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-028]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper claims that its variational algorithm requires O(d log(1/ε)) qubits and O(poly(d log(1/ε))) few-qubit gates, suggesting feasibility on small-scale quantum hardware, and that the SWAP-test-based inner product estimation avoids measurement complexity factors of the form (1/ε)^{O(d)}, yielding an overall measurement complexity scaling of O(1/ε² (log(1/ε))^d). They derive measurement costs within VQS, showing that the number of measurements for Hadamard-test-based quantities scales as O(|ψ₀(t)|²/ε̄²), and argue that the SWAP test’s measurement count NSWAP does not include exponential-in-d precision factors. In numerical simulations on a single-asset double knock-out barrier option, they validate that increasing the number of grid points/qubits (ngr) leads to solutions closer to the analytical solution and that increasing ansatz depth improves agreement with classical FDM. They also demonstrate that the payoff-encoded initial state can be well approximated by a variational ansatz with very high fidelity, reporting an initial-state approximation error around 1.2×10⁻⁵, and interpret this as the fidelity asymptotically converging to 1.
    [codes: C-003, C-010, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors explicitly compare their approach to classical finite difference methods, noting that classical FDM has time and space complexity O((1/ε)^{O(d)}) due to the underlying grid dimension O((1/ε)^{d/2}), whereas their quantum method uses O(d log(1/ε)) qubits to encode the same grid and avoids a (1/ε)^{O(d)} measurement factor in the SWAP test. In numerical experiments on the double-barrier option, they observe that as the number of grid points (ngr) grows, their VQS-based solution behaves similarly to classical FDM, in the sense that larger ngr yields solutions closer to the analytical solution, and that deeper ansatzes better approximate classical FDM results.
    [codes: C-005, C-021, C-019, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations and caveats. First, prior ‘naive’ quantum PDE approaches suffer from an exponential measurement cost because the derivative price resides in a single amplitude, and even in their framework, if the intermediate future time t_ter is chosen too small, the quantum speedup is lost and the situation reverts to extracting one amplitude. They stress that their complexity claims assume that the initial BSPDE state and the probability-distribution state can be efficiently generated by some variational algorithms and that all required state-preparation unitaries are O(poly(d log(1/ε))), which is an assumption not proved in the paper. The authors also note that not performing a log transformation is a modeling restriction stemming from their formulation being able to handle only boundary conditions linear in the asset prices si. They clarify that their initial-state-fitting optimization does not correspond to real physical operations, i.e., it is a classical optimization demonstration rather than an implemented quantum routine, and that an efficient search algorithm for such initial-state parameters is not provided. More broadly, they concede in the conclusion that they simply assumed efficient state preparation for both the payoff-encoded initial state and the probability-embedded state, leaving this key requirement unresolved.
    [codes: C-006, C-012, C-023, C-024, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors explicitly identify the need to design an efficient algorithm to search for ansatz parameters that prepare the required initial payoff state, stating that they leave the construction of such an efficient search method to future research. They also implicitly point to developing concrete, physically realizable state-preparation routines that satisfy their efficiency assumptions for both the initial BSPDE state and the probability-distribution state.
    [codes: C-035, C-036]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in applying variational quantum simulation to the Black–Scholes PDE for multi-asset derivatives and in formulating the derivative price as an inner product between the PDE solution and a probability distribution, computed via a SWAP test to avoid the amplitude-extraction measurement bottleneck found in naive quantum approaches. They position this as yielding a potential quantum speedup—even on noisy, small-scale devices—by achieving qubit counts of O(d log(1/ε)) and eliminating (1/ε)^{O(d)} factors in the measurement complexity, while extending their prior work that expressed present derivative prices as expectations of discounted future prices.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-025]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is primarily theoretical with numerical simulations, not hardware experiments, and uses a well-specified finite-difference discretization where the state dimension scales as O((1/ε)^{d/2}). The authors clearly describe their algorithmic pipeline, including how to prepare the probability-encoding state, apply VQS to the BSPDE, and perform the SWAP test for inner-product estimation. They provide an analytical benchmark via a known closed-form solution for the single-asset double-barrier option and report how numerical accuracy improves with more grid points and ansatz layers. For the initial-state preparation subproblem, they treat the optimization as a classical procedure, emphasizing that this does not correspond to real physical operations and explicitly leaving efficient quantum search for such parameters to future work. Overall, they are transparent about measurement cost formulas in VQS and SWAP tests and about the assumptions underlying their complexity estimates.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-021, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper discusses a tradeoff in selecting the intermediate future time t_ter used in the martingale-based pricing identity, recommending that t_ter be taken as large as possible while keeping the approximation between two derived expressions valid; this choice interacts with both the quality of the pricing approximation and the maintenance of potential quantum speedup. It also notes a modeling choice to omit a log transformation of asset prices because their variational formulation can only accommodate boundary conditions linear in si.
    [codes: C-011, C-014]

=== PAPER 4d07c1a00ccf (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets pricing of European and arithmetic Asian options under the Black–Scholes model by solving the associated linear pricing PDEs via a quantum approach. It motivates this by noting that classical numerical PDE and related methods become computationally intensive, particularly as model complexity and dimensionality increase, leading to a curse-of-dimensionality issue for products such as baskets. The PDEs are reformulated through variable changes into heat-equation form and, for Asians, a time-dependent PDE, which are then cast into an imaginary-time Schrödinger equation suitable for quantum treatment.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-040]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a hybrid quantum–classical algorithm, adapted from quantum chemistry, that uses quantum imaginary-time evolution to approximate solutions of the pricing PDEs. They exploit the equivalence between the heat-equation form of the pricing PDE and the Schrödinger equation in imaginary time, apply a Wick rotation, and approximate the evolving state with a parameterised ansatz circuit built from a shallow, few-qubit architecture using real-valued Ry-based gates. The variational parameters follow an ODE system derived from McLachlan’s variational principle, with matrices A and C measured on a quantum device, parameters updated classically via an Euler scheme and least-squares stabilization, and, for the Asian case, a discretisation that freezes the time-dependent Hamiltonian on each time interval.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On a 4-qubit, shallow ansatz circuit corresponding to a 16-point grid, the authors report that their method can reconstruct the imaginary-time evolution of the European call option pricing state with small norm errors and that quantum-simulated prices at inception and maturity agree well with classical PDE solutions. They further claim that the same shallow circuit suffices to price both European and arithmetic Asian options in the Black–Scholes model with very good accuracy, and emphasize as an operational advantage that all required matrix elements for the variational ODEs can be measured on a quantum computer.
    [codes: C-025, C-030, C-034, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum approach is benchmarked against classical PDE solvers by comparing option prices and state-vector evolutions; the authors state that the quantum-simulated prices at maturity and inception match the expected classical solutions and that state errors remain small. In the broader context, they contrast their method with prior quantum option-pricing work based on amplitude estimation, which they note can yield quadratic speed-ups over classical Monte Carlo, and they position their PDE-based scheme as an alternative route that may be competitive where classical PDE methods become computationally intensive.
    [codes: C-005, C-007, C-008, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations. First, the variational ODE system involves a matrix A(τ) that is often ill-conditioned, requiring a regularized least-squares solution and an eigenvalue cut-off, signalling numerical stability concerns. Second, the initial-state fitting problem for the payoff is non-convex, so care is needed in optimization and there is no guarantee of finding a good parameter set; if the chosen ansatz cannot approximate the payoff state well, the authors concede that running the time evolution becomes pointless unless a more expressive or tailored ansatz is devised. Third, they note an algorithmic caveat that their methodology only checks quantum approximation accuracy at the payoff (boundary) level, which may fail when the price function varies significantly over time, raising the risk of undetected error propagation in the intermediate evolution.
    [codes: C-022, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors suggest exploring imaginary-time evolution algorithms that bypass the variational ansatz and its associated optimisation, as potential routes to more scalable implementations. They also stress the need to design more efficient ansätze tailored to complex financial products or to move towards ansatz-free approaches. As a key application direction, they highlight basket options involving multiple underlying assets as a promising extension, especially since such multidimensional problems are particularly challenging for classical PDE methods.

  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper’s claimed contribution is a hybrid quantum–classical algorithm, inspired by quantum-chemistry imaginary-time techniques, for pricing linear PDE-based derivatives—specifically European and arithmetic Asian options—using shallow circuits on only a few qubits. By leveraging the equivalence between pricing PDEs and the imaginary-time Schrödinger equation and constructing a custom shallow ansatz tailored to this real-valued evolution, the authors position their scheme as a promising candidate for applying noisy, near-term quantum hardware to quantitative finance.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-016, C-024, C-026, C-037]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is implemented as a hybrid variational scheme in which quantum hardware (or a simulator) is used only to measure expectation values defining matrices A and C, while parameter updates and time integration are performed classically via an Euler scheme and regularized linear solves. The authors provide an explicit description of the quantum notation and gate model used, specify the gate set and ansatz structure, and discuss practical numerical issues such as matrix conditioning and initialization accuracy, but there is no mention of real-device experiments or code release, suggesting that results are obtained on ideal simulators and that reproducibility depends on reimplementation from the described circuits and procedures.

=== PAPER 4de005c12725 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets quantum speedup for Monte Carlo–based derivative pricing by using amplitude estimation within quantum Monte Carlo integration (QMCI) to improve the convergence rate, focusing on efficient implementation of repeatedly used payoff functions as state-dependent unitaries on a quantum device. It formulates the pricing of European vanilla and basket options as expectation estimation problems where the key bottleneck is constructing a resource-efficient quantum circuit for the payoff operator F acting on discretized asset-price registers. The authors frame this as a function-approximation and state-preparation problem under NISQ hardware constraints, where quantum circuits must be extremely resource-efficient to be practical.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-018, C-036, C-042]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is built around parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) used as function approximators for payoff functions, which are then converted into conditional parameterized quantum circuits (CPQCs) that implement state-dependent operations controlled by a basis-encoded register representing random variables. The authors define CPQCs formally and derive a construction where encoding subcircuits in a trained PQC are replaced by controlled versions that receive inputs from a joint distribution loaded into the control register; for rotational encodings, they show an efficient implementation via uniformly controlled rotations whose gate count scales linearly with the number of control qubits. A key ingredient is a genetic, hardware-aware architecture search that alternates adding/removing parameterized and encoding blocks, uses mutation and selection with inverse-squared-cost weighting, and restricts building blocks so learned PQCs can be transformed into CPQCs; this framework is then used to implement F for option payoffs via angle encodings of prices and (for some experiments) weights.
    [codes: C-003, C-012, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-043, C-046]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim that their CPQC-based implementation of option payoffs yields more resource-efficient circuits (in CNOT count and depth) than previously existing quantum algorithms based on explicit quantum arithmetic, with asymptotically linear gate scaling in the number of qubits n for both the conditional construction and specific payoff classes. For basket options with fixed weights, they analytically contrast the O(n log n) complexity of the baseline arithmetic implementation with an O(n) total gate complexity for their CPQC, and empirically report reduced CNOT counts and depth for European vanilla options as well. They further highlight that the overhead for reusing a trained PQC in conditional form scales only linearly in the discretization qubit count and that in the variable-weight basket experiment the learned circuit structure encodes the weight only once and appears to implement a rotation of the payoff function that the PQC can represent well.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-010, C-014, C-028, C-039, C-041, C-044, C-045, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: At the algorithmic level, the work is motivated by the theoretical quadratic improvement in convergence rate of quantum amplitude estimation over classical Monte Carlo for expectation estimation tasks such as derivative pricing. Within the quantum domain, the authors benchmark their CPQC-based function implementation against a baseline that uses explicit quantum arithmetic, including comparator circuits and a weighted-sum register for basket options, noting that the arithmetic method scales as O(n) for vanilla options and O(n log n) for fixed-weight baskets. Their CPQC constructions are reported to require fewer CNOT gates and shallower depth than these arithmetic baselines for the considered discretizations, but direct runtime or error comparisons to purely classical pricing implementations are not provided.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-038, C-039, C-043, C-044, C-041, C-045]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several important limitations. First, using PQCs as universal function approximators generally requires high-depth circuits to achieve good approximation quality, which is problematic on NISQ devices with high error rates. Second, the naive or “trivial” construction of CPQCs via fully controlled versions of encoding gates incurs exponential gate cost, motivating the need for more efficient constructions. Third, their resource reduction strategy comes at the price of computationally expensive classical pretraining; for instance, the genetic search in one experiment took about 5.5 hours on a large classical server, underscoring a nontrivial classical overhead. Finally, the authors explicitly state that the additional approximation error introduced by PQC-based function implementation must be traded off against gate-count reductions, and that determining the level of gate reduction at which this extra error is justified remains an open question.
    [codes: C-008, C-020, C-026, C-040, C-050]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors indicate that a key direction for future work is to systematically study and quantify the tradeoff between reduced gate counts and the additional approximation error introduced by PQC/CPQC-based function implementations, in order to determine under what resource reductions this extra error is justified for practical applications.
    [codes: C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in presenting a method that substantially reduces quantum resources needed for implementing state-dependent payoff functions by offloading complexity to classical pretraining, thereby avoiding the need to hand-design payoff circuits and evading typical data-loading bottlenecks found in many QML settings. It introduces the formal notion of conditional parameterized quantum circuits and proves that matching expectations in the QMCI setting follows from matching individual encodings, enabling an efficient conditional variant for PQCs that use specific rotational encodings with only linear overhead in the number of discretization qubits. Additionally, the authors propose a tailored, hardware-aware genetic architecture search that extends variable-ansatz techniques to include encoding blocks and enforces CPQC-compatibility, yielding payoff circuits that, for basket options, achieve better asymptotic and empirical gate scaling than existing quantum arithmetic approaches.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-045]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work combines theoretical analysis of CPQC constructions with empirical evaluation on simulated NISQ-style devices, but does not discuss noise or real-hardware runs, relying instead on idealized simulations. The genetic structure-learning procedure is described in detail, including the alternation of block addition and gate removal, the inclusion of encoding blocks that relax identity-parameter constraints to enhance expressivity, and hardware-aware constraints that restrict blocks to native gates and physical connectivity, improving practical relevance. Selection in the genetic algorithm is formalized via inverse-squared-cost weighting, and CPQC-compatibility is enforced by only permitting blocks of a specific structure, which enhances the reproducibility of the architecture search logic, though no code release is mentioned and dataset size/details for training discretizations are only implicitly defined. The authors also conceptually justify their CPQC design by noting the absence of phase-kickback errors from repeated controlling and by clearly specifying an efficiency criterion based on linear gate scaling in n.
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The authors make two additional qualitative observations: in the variable-weight basket option case, the learned circuit encodes the weight only once, and visually the circuit seems to act by rotating the payoff function in a way the PQC can represent well, offering interpretability insights into the learned quantum model. They also emphasize that their construction of CPQCs avoids unintentional phase-kickback errors that might otherwise arise from repeatedly controlled operations.
    [codes: C-025, C-047, C-048]

=== PAPER 50989fdc9ad1 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the core obstacle for quantum algorithms in finance and statistics as the lack of efficient, updatable state-preparation routines for loading classical probability distributions into quantum states, particularly when worst‑case arbitrary states are prohibitively deep and ancilla‑intensive and when existing methods require updating many circuit parameters each time model parameters change (C-001, C-002, C-004). It formulates the problem as preparing quantum states that encode statistical distributions and mixtures, Odistr|0⟩ = ∑x p(x)|x⟩, with p(x) arising from parametric or maximum‑entropy models, and then using these states for downstream tasks like derivative pricing and risk analysis (C-012, C-035, C-038).
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-012, C-035, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors introduce a statistics‑informed parameterized quantum circuit (SI‑PQC) framework that links quantum state preparation to intrinsic statistical symmetries via the maximum entropy principle, using observables with conservative expectations as symmetry‑defining constraints (C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015). Within this framework, they decompose distributional information into fixed constraint functions fk (encoding prior model knowledge) and tunable parameters λk (encoding data uncertainty), and implement a maximum entropy distribution loader (MEDL) in three steps: unitary dilation of normalized constraint functions, linear combination of these via block encoding, and QSVT‑based imaginary‑time evolution to approximate the exponential form (C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020). The circuit architecture is a static state‑preparation structure with model parameters explicitly encoded as rotation angles, enabling reuse, deep compilation, and compatibility with a weighted distribution mixer (WDM) that reuses MEDL components and encodes parameter uncertainty in latent registers for mixture models, as well as with a variational learning protocol and QMCI/QAE for finance applications (C-009, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-037, C-038).
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-009, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-029, C-030, C-035, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that SI‑PQC, via MEDL, achieves universal expressiveness with an optimally dimensioned learning space and classical preprocessing complexity that is optimal in the number of model parameters M, since only O(M) rotation angles must be updated (C-011, C-019). For single distributions, the MEDL theorem gives single‑shot circuit depth O(n M df log(1/ε)) with success probability F²/4, improved to depth O(n M df log(1/ε)/F) with amplitude amplification, and analogous complexity bounds hold for mixtures under the WDM theorem with only logarithmic additional depth in the number of mixture components (C-021, C-022, C-026, C-028). SI‑PQC‑based learning is argued to reduce training complexity and improve generalization because it uses only Npara = M ≪ n independent gates and a repetition count Nrepeat independent of qubit number, leading to generalization error bounds driven by the small parameter count (C-033, C-034). In finance applications, the authors state that QMCI with SI‑PQC enables a quantum extension of incremental computing for pricing, yielding a favorable end‑to‑end resource expression, and that Greeks can be obtained directly via parameter‑shift rules on the SI‑PQC parameters (C-035, C-036, C-037). For risk analysis, they show numerically that slowly varying observables such as E[X] and E[ln X] serve as conservative constraints and that SI‑PQC can efficiently and accurately approximate empirical distributions to recover quantities like empirical VaR from simulated data (C-039, C-040).
    [codes: C-011, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-026, C-028, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to classical or existing quantum‑assisted pipelines that rely on heavy preprocessing, the authors argue that a static SI‑PQC structure with only M tunable parameters avoids recomputing large preprocessed artifacts and thus preserves potential speed‑ups in time‑dependent models (C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-023). For mixture models, they explicitly contrast WDM with straightforward QSP+LCU combinations that require Nθ repetitions of full circuits, claiming that WDM needs only logarithmic additional depth, leading to an exponential reduction in time and quantum resources for mixtures (C-006, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-010). In learning, they position SI‑PQC favorably against generic QML models whose generalization error scales with a larger parameter count, emphasizing that SI‑PQC uses only M independent gates (C-033, C-034). In pricing and VaR estimation, SI‑PQC‑based QMCI is presented as a quantum analogue of classical incremental computing and classical Monte Carlo, with the resource expression TTSSI−PQC intended to be lower end‑to‑end than approaches where state preparation dominates (C-035, C-036).
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-009, C-019, C-023, C-006, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-010, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that classical pre-processing approaches are fragile in time‑dependent settings because previously computed artifacts quickly become obsolete, erasing any prospective quantum speed‑ups; SI‑PQC is partly motivated as a remedy but they treat this as a limitation of many current methods (C-005). They also note that a simple combination of QSP routines with LCU for mixtures incurs prohibitive overhead, motivating but not fully eliminating mixture‑model complexity concerns (C-006). For their own proposal, they state that for small qubit numbers n, the asymptotic resource advantage of SI‑PQC can be diminished by larger constant prefactors, so practical gains may only materialize at moderate or large scales (C-041). They further mention that block‑encoding of certain linear functions can be viewed as a limitation of SI‑PQC, suggesting the need to hybridize with pre‑trained PQCs to address this gap (C-042).

  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: As a way to mitigate current limitations in implementing linear functions within SI‑PQC, the authors suggest combining SI‑PQC with a pre‑trained PQC used specifically for block encoding, effectively proposing hybrid architectures as future work (C-042). They also state that SI‑PQC could be extended beyond the paper’s concrete tasks to loading and simulating time series and to designing quantum algorithms for non‑parametric and semi‑parametric statistical tests, indicating broader statistical and financial applications (C-043). Additionally, they point to a possible but unexplored connection between SI‑PQC and quantum state tomography or verification, explicitly leaving this line of inquiry open (C-044).
    [codes: C-042, C-043, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in introducing a statistics‑informed parameterized quantum circuit that embeds prior knowledge about data symmetries via observables with conservative expectations and the maximum entropy principle, yielding maximum‑entropy distributions as the ‘best unbiased guess’ when explicit formulas are unavailable (C-007, C-008, C-014, C-015, C-016).   DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the framework is grounded in a clear separation between fixed prior knowledge (encoded in constraint functions fk) and tunable data‑driven parameters λk, which dictates both circuit design and learning strategy and is explicitly aligned with the maximum entropy principle (C-014, C-015, C-016). [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as a technology with the potential to transform finance broadly, given that any computation‑intensive financial task could benefit from quantum speed‑ups, and notes a wide variety of proposed applications despite the early technological stage. It structures the problem space into three principal methodological application areas—optimization, Monte Carlo methods, and machine learning—across financial domains such as asset management, investment banking, and retail/corporate banking, and then focuses on concrete use cases like portfolio optimization, transaction settlement, derivative pricing, risk measurement, and financial crash prediction. The authors emphasize potential financial benefits (e.g., enhanced investment gains, reduced capital requirements, improved risk management and compliance) but acknowledge that literature quantifying impacts and monetary benefits is still scarce.
    [codes: C-001, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-051]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: Methodologically, the survey develops a four‑layer comparison framework spanning use case, methodology (optimization, simulation/Monte Carlo, and machine learning), algorithmic layer, and hardware layer, with upper layers tied to financial tasks and lower layers to technical implementation. At the algorithmic level, most applications rely on a small set of known quantum algorithms to obtain speed‑ups—particularly amplitude estimation for Monte Carlo‑style pricing and risk analysis, quantum annealing and QUBO/Ising formulations for optimization, and gate‑based variational approaches—while the hardware layer records whether implementations target gate‑based devices or quantum annealers. The authors explicitly exclude quantum‑inspired classical methods such as tensor networks from the scope of the survey and note that some hardware constraints (e.g., limited connectivity, errors) can be partially mitigated in software, including via swap operations and quantum error correction, albeit with costs.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-039, C-049, C-052, C-056, C-005, C-009, C-010, C-011]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: From 13 selected application papers, the survey reports that optimization dominates (8/13 papers), followed by Monte Carlo‑based simulations (6/13), with no concrete machine‑learning use cases identified. Hardware‑wise, four implementations target quantum annealers and nine target gate‑based devices, with gate‑based systems covering both optimization and Monte Carlo use cases. Reported performance highlights include quantum annealers that can already approach commercial solvers on small portfolio optimization tasks, reverse annealing being empirically over 100× faster than forward annealing, theoretical better‑than‑classical scaling for a quantum SOCP‑based portfolio optimizer, and quadratic theoretical speed‑ups via amplitude estimation for derivative pricing and risk/VaR/CVaR estimation; on real hardware, simple error‑mitigation techniques reduced option‑pricing errors from 62% to 21%.
    [codes: C-024, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-045, C-052, C-053, C-056, C-063]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Several surveyed studies explicitly compare quantum and classical approaches: portfolio optimization implementations benchmark quantum methods against conventional commercial solvers, with some quantum annealers approaching their performance on small instances. The survey notes that theoretical analyses often claim improved asymptotic complexity (e.g., better‑scaling quantum SOCP solvers, quadratic improvements in sample complexity for quantum amplitude estimation over classical Monte Carlo), but also emphasizes that Monte Carlo can be massively parallelized classically, which raises the practical threshold for quantum advantage. Overall, the authors stress that many purported quantum advantages are at this stage theoretical or demonstrated only on toy problems, and that further investigation is needed to establish robust advantage over classical tools.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-042, C-045, C-046, C-052, C-056, C-058, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The survey emphasizes substantial limitations: current quantum hardware is hard to scale, requires more qubits with lower error rates, and existing experiments often exhaust available qubit counts, connectivity, and gate fidelity, making typical industry‑scale portfolios or realistic networks infeasible on present devices. Simulation of quantum computers on classical hardware is exponentially expensive in qubit number, and software workarounds such as swap operations or error correction introduce additional operations, noise, and qubit overhead. Many reported advantages are only theoretical or on very low‑complexity examples; speed‑ups often depend on problem‑specific parameters, and classical Monte Carlo’s massive parallelizability further raises the bar for quantum advantage. Financially, portfolio optimization with realistic constraints lacks closed‑form solutions, crash prediction is characterized as extremely difficult and almost unsolvable for classical computers, and for many proposed use cases no robust back‑testing or real‑world validation exists yet. At a market level, the authors stress that literature quantifying the economic impacts or monetary benefits of quantum computing in finance is scarce, hardware breakthroughs and economic/cost‑effective operation are needed to realize potential, and it remains very difficult to estimate when sufficiently powerful quantum technology will be available.

  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest that noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) devices may deliver useful financial applications before fully fault‑tolerant machines are available, implying a need to explore NISQ‑compatible algorithms and hybrid strategies. They call for further investigation to clarify whether approaches like QAOA/quantum alternating operator ansatz can genuinely yield quantum advantage in realistic portfolio rebalancing, and stress that crash‑prediction methods must be rigorously back‑tested to validate predictive power. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The work targets quantum enhancements for core quantitative finance tasks, specifically derivative pricing and Value at Risk (VaR), by formulating them as expectation‑estimation problems amenable to Quantum Accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) and amplitude estimation; VaR/Expected Shortfall is further reduced to a pricing‑type problem by encoding a step function oracle whose measurement probabilities correspond to tail probabilities of the loss distribution.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-021]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors study QAMC with a "standard encoding" and propose a modified encoding plus a new Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (RQAE) algorithm. The standard encoding prepares a superposition matching classical path probabilities and uses an oracle to encode payoffs, with amplitude estimation providing the quadratic Monte Carlo speedup; the new encoding instead directly loads probabilities and payoffs (not their square roots) and adds one extra qubit, while RQAE is designed to estimate both amplitude magnitude and sign by being sensitive to the underlying phase. They emphasize that oracle efficiency and the tunable depth–accuracy trade‑off in RQAE (via parameter q) are central to overall algorithmic performance.
    [codes: C-002, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-027, C-028, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that the new encoding and RQAE enable pricing of derivatives and other financial products with negative payoffs or values, where standard encodings fail: the new encoding converges to the correct Riemann sum for negative payoffs, and RQAE is the only tested AE variant that converges to the exact solution on a negative‑price example. Quantitatively, they restate that QAMC with amplitude estimation yields a Monte Carlo error scaling of order 1/Noracle, and they find that RQAE attains performance similar to well‑known AE algorithms in terms of convergence behavior.
    [codes: C-004, C-005, C-018, C-026, C-030, C-034, C-007]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to classical Monte Carlo, the authors highlight the known quadratic improvement in error scaling when using amplitude estimation, contrasting the classical ε_MC ∼ 1/√Npaths and overall ε ∼ 1/√C behavior with the quantum ε_MC ∼ 1/Noracle scaling, under the usual assumptions about oracle efficiency. They stress, however, that despite this theoretical advantage, their concrete algorithms—especially when implemented on current NISQ devices—are not yet competitive with classical Monte Carlo methods in practical pricing and VaR computations.
    [codes: C-002, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-018, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors underscore multiple limitations. First, the new encoding suffers from a large constant‑factor overhead proportional to Npaths, which can overshadow or even nullify the quadratic speedup and yields worse performance than the standard encoding in many settings. Second, their proposals are not yet applicable or competitive on current NISQ hardware due to excessive qubit requirements for oracles, circuit depths incompatible with decoherence times, and gate counts that demand error rates beyond today’s capabilities. Third, while RQAE matches other AE algorithms in asymptotic performance and uniquely handles negative amplitudes, it often requires more oracle calls than the most advanced competitors, further limiting its practicality.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-031, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future research, the authors call for improved stochastic differential equation (SDE) solvers tailored to quantum Monte Carlo pipelines and, critically, new techniques to implement oracles with significantly reduced depth and qubit counts. They frame the main ongoing challenge as simultaneously advancing these algorithmic and implementation aspects so that QAMC‑based pricing and risk algorithms become more realistic for future hardware.
    [codes: C-037, C-038]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims two primary contributions: a new encoding protocol for QAMC and a new Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (RQAE) algorithm. The encoding is presented as a way to correctly handle payoffs that can take negative values by loading payoffs and probabilities directly, while RQAE is introduced as an AE variant explicitly sensitive to amplitude sign (via phase information), enabling pricing of financial products with negative values. They further argue that RQAE achieves convergence comparable to state‑of‑the‑art AE algorithms while adding this sign‑sensitivity capability.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-028, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-007]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the study builds on the standard Riemann‑sum discretization of payoff expectations and makes explicit the error‑scaling analysis for both classical Monte Carlo and quantum amplitude estimation, which clarifies the theoretical benchmark. The authors also discuss in detail where standard encoding fails—through the absolute‑value effect in the amplitudes—and how the new encoding plus RQAE fix this on test problems, indicating a careful diagnostic of algorithmic failure modes rather than only showcasing successful cases.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper highlights that the efficiency of the state‑preparation oracle is a key determinant of end‑to‑end performance in QAMC, and that RQAE’s tunable parameter q introduces an explicit trade‑off between circuit depth and convergence speed, offering a knob for adapting to different hardware constraints.

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper conceptually frames quantum calculus (q- and h-calculus) as a way to extend classical calculus to discrete or finite settings and then explores how q-derivatives and q-integrals could support financial modeling tasks such as derivative pricing, risk sensitivities (Greeks), and handling jump processes in stochastic/financial mathematics. It positions finance as one among several application domains where these discrete, limit-free tools and their quantum-computing-enabled implementations may offer more accurate or efficient computation, particularly for complex derivatives and models with discontinuities.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-040, C-047, C-048]

They claim that combining q-derivatives and discrete models with quantum algorithms enables direct gradient estimation and parallel evaluation of many price paths, and more broadly argue that quantum calculus provides a unified framework for fundamental quantum-computing operations (unitaries and projective measurements) and for designing quantum algorithms across paradigms.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-045, C-046, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-054]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper is conceptual and does not report implemented financial experiments or numerical benchmarks; instead it restates known theoretical speedups and qualitative advantages. It notes that q-analogs and q-difference equations generalize classical structures and appear broadly across mathematics and physics, that q-integrals can be viewed as q-analogs of Riemann–Stieltjes integrals and could be more accurate and faster for financial computations with jumps, and that combining q-derivatives with quantum algorithms has been applied in discrete-model fields to improve efficiency and accuracy. For finance specifically, the authors claim potential benefits such as more efficient computation of sensitivities (Greeks) via quantum gradient algorithms and a quadratic reduction in simulation counts (from O(1/ε²) to O(1/ε)) for high-accuracy derivative pricing when using quantum amplitude estimation.

  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors contrast their quantum-calculus-plus-quantum-computing perspective with classical methods at several points. They emphasize that q-difference equations and q-integrals are generalizations of classical differential and Riemann(-Stieltjes) integrals that better handle discrete jumps and non-smooth functions, where classical numerical methods can fail or be less accurate. For financial derivatives, they highlight that classical Monte Carlo pricing requires O(1/ε²) paths versus O(1/ε) queries under quantum amplitude estimation, and that classical finite-difference estimation of Greeks is computationally expensive because it requires many revaluations, whereas quantum gradient algorithms in principle estimate gradients directly and in superposition. At the modeling level, it notes that classical Riemann integration fails to operate well when the integrator has jumps or discontinuities and that other numerical methods can struggle with discrete jumps and non-smooth functions, motivating but not yet empirically validating the use of q-integrals. At the hardware and algorithmic level, the authors stress that quantum error correction remains an important unsolved problem, decoherence degrades quantum states and limits stability and practicality, and that as a consequence the full power of quantum computing—particularly robust quantum supremacy over classical systems—still falls short in practice. They also implicitly recognize that current scalable, robust qubit architectures are lacking and must be developed before the proposed advantages can be fully realized.
