They also mention ongoing research into the role of Mersenne primes in post-quantum cryptography and imply that further exploration of quantum-calculus-based formulations (e.g., for integrals and discrete models) in finance and cryptography could be fruitful once more capable quantum hardware and error correction techniques are in place.

Within this, it highlights the connection between q-integrals and Riemann–Stieltjes integrals via step functions with jumps at q-points, and it sketches how q-derivatives and q-Riemann–Stieltjes integrals could be applied in financial mathematics for discrete, jump-driven models and in conjunction with known quantum algorithms (QAE and quantum gradient methods) to potentially improve pricing and risk management. The method discretizes the terminal price interval into 2^n grid points represented on n qubits, stores probabilities as amplitudes, uses auxiliary qubits and a comparator to implement the payoff, and then runs QAE to extract the payoff-related amplitude, with state preparation reflecting a truncated lognormal distribution in the simple option case.

=== PAPER 5f3cabc4cfc6 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames European call option pricing as an early high-value application of quantum computing in finance, motivated by the expectation that the financial sector may be among the first to benefit from increased quantum computational power. It focuses on computing the discounted expected payoff of a European call, under a Black–Scholes–Merton geometric Brownian motion model with log-normal terminal asset prices, while acknowledging that real-world, path-dependent derivatives are substantially more complex targets than the simple European option considered. The work is explicitly positioned as an introductory tutorial that explains financial derivatives basics and then formulates the European option pricing problem for a qudit-based quantum computer.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-010]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors build on quantum Monte Carlo-style pricing using quantum amplitude estimation, adapting the standard qubit-based framework to a qudit register. They prepare a "probability" register of qudits into a weighted superposition encoding the discretized log-normal asset price distribution, using an affine mapping from computational basis states to asset prices and Householder transformations for state preparation. The method then applies a comparator that flips an ancilla qubit based on whether the encoded asset price exceeds the strike and uses controlled-Y rotations to encode a scaled and shifted payoff into an ancilla, followed by amplitude amplification via a Grover-type rotation and maximum-likelihood-based amplitude estimation that avoids explicit phase estimation.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that, in numerical simulations, the qudit-based pricing pipeline yields an estimated option payoff whose value rapidly approaches both the payoff computed on a similarly resourced classical computer and the analytic "true" payoff, once the qudit dimension is modestly increased. Analytically, the authors reiterate that classical Monte Carlo pricing has an estimator error scaling as O(M^{-1/2}), while quantum amplitude estimation achieves O(M^{-1}), and they state that their maximum-likelihood version of amplitude estimation asymptotically preserves this O(M^{-1}) error scaling in the number of oracle calls. They further note that the BSM-based log-normal distribution design permits efficient state preparation in this setting, which underpins the feasibility of their simulated scheme.
    [codes: C-004, C-008, C-013, C-014, C-024, C-034, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical Monte Carlo integration is used conceptually as the main baseline, with the authors recalling its O(M^{-1/2}) convergence in estimator error and positioning quantum amplitude estimation as offering a quadratic O(M^{-1}) improvement in this metric. In addition, in their simulations they compare the qudit-based scheme’s estimated payoff to that produced by a classical method operating on a finite, similarly discretized asset-price grid, as well as to the analytic payoff from the continuous BSM model, and they report close agreement as qudit dimension increases.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-035, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge multiple limitations and bottlenecks. First, they note that standard quantum amplitude estimation is practically constrained because the phase estimation subroutine and associated quantum Fourier transform are prohibitively expensive on current hardware, making them a key bottleneck. They also emphasize that naively repeating state preparation and measuring the payoff qubit does not yield any quantum advantage over classical Monte Carlo, so more sophisticated amplitude estimation is required. On the modeling side, they acknowledge the need to truncate the theoretically unbounded asset price domain to a finite interval that captures most of the probability mass, which introduces approximation error, and they rely on small-angle approximations when recovering the payoff from ancilla measurement probabilities. At the circuit level, they point out that generic qubit and qudit state preparation and arbitrary unitary decomposition have poor scaling—exponential in system size for straightforward schemes and O(n d^n) primitive operations for arbitrary qudit unitaries—highlighting that their construction is only tractable because of special structure in the distribution. They also identify the phase-estimation part of QAE (and, more generally, phase estimation and inverse quantum Fourier transform) as primary experimental bottlenecks for derivative pricing implementations.
    [codes: C-015, C-018, C-022, C-023, C-033, C-035, C-037]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper suggests that machine learning techniques, which are used classically for density estimation and probabilistic modeling, could similarly be leveraged in the quantum setting to encode complex distributions into quantum states, indicating a future research direction towards quantum machine learning-based distribution loading for more realistic derivative pricing problems.
    [codes: C-025]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors position their work as an introductory, tutorial-style exposition that both explains the basics of financial derivatives to quantum computing enthusiasts and provides a detailed description of the qudit-based algorithmic routines needed to price a European option. Their contribution also includes adapting the standard quantum Monte Carlo derivative pricing framework to higher-dimensional qudits, emphasizing the logarithmic information capacity, potential noise robustness, and hardware-native implementations of qudit gates, and demonstrating numerically that a qudit-based stack can approximate both classical finite-resource and analytic payoffs with modest qudit dimension. They further highlight the use of maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation without phase estimation within this qudit architecture as a more experimentally accessible route to quadratic Monte Carlo speedup.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-011, C-016, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper is structured as a didactic walkthrough of the full pricing stack, specifying the mathematical formulation of the option payoff and its discounted expectation, the Black–Scholes–Merton model assumption, and the derivation of the log-normal terminal price distribution. It carefully describes the discretization of the continuous distribution onto a finite qudit register, including truncation choices, affine mapping to asset prices, and state-preparation via Householder transformations, as well as the construction of comparator and payoff-encoding subcircuits and the relationship between ancilla measurement probabilities and the encoded payoff. The authors also discuss algorithmic scaling and implementation complexity for generic state preparation and qudit decompositions, and they motivate parameter choices for the maximum-likelihood amplitude estimation schedule, but the work remains entirely simulation-based without hardware experiments, and circuit resource counts are mostly discussed at the scaling level rather than as full reproducibility-ready gate tallies.

  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates the proposed qudit-based methods within the context of emerging hardware platforms by noting that analogues of X, Z, and CZ gates for qudits are naturally supported in linear ion-trap and multi-port photonic architectures, and by highlighting cavity-based control schemes (such as SNAP and displacement gates) as a promising alternative that can implement arbitrary operations on cavity-qudit/transmon systems. A key ingredient is a seed‑based random‑number generation mechanism combined with quantum rejection sampling to shape the distribution of increments, and the architecture is extended by adding registers and controlled interactions for multiple correlated stochastic variables (e.g., Heston volatility) and for nested risk analysis via a secondary index register.
    [codes: C-004, C-015, C-016, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-037, C-039]

Simulation studies report that pricing error increases with asset volatility, decreases with the number of simulated paths in a manner approximated by an error ∝ 1/N relationship, and plateaus beyond about 100 time steps, while increasing precision bits initially yields a sharp improvement and is speculated to induce an exponentially decaying error with precision. For multivariate extensions, they assert that adding each new stochastic variable increases the qubit count only linearly.

Within their own method, they explicitly acknowledge that the proposed seed‑based quantum random number generation and rejection‑sampling operator has not been fully validated and that further work is needed to demonstrate its efficiency and randomness quality. A central design choice is to compute stopping times via dynamic programming in superposition across all stochastic paths, implemented through specific unitaries and circuits, and supported by controlled rotations and a quantum Monte Carlo subroutine, while much of the linear-algebra postprocessing (e.g., matrix inversion) remains classical.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-029, C-030, C-034]

It provides formal error bounds that separate sampling error from an approximation term depending on how well polynomial basis functions approximate continuation values, and derives explicit quantum complexity expressions, including specialised bounds for Brownian motion where orthonormal Hermite bases make key matrices the identity and improve runtime, and for geometric Brownian motion where Vandermonde structure and singular-value bounds govern complexity. The main theorems and corollaries articulate quantum runtime scaling, asymptotic complexity under smoothness, and settings where the sought-after quadratic improvement in ε is achieved.

They provide a formal classical correctness and complexity theorem and emphasise that the quantum advantage is specifically in the reduced number of oracle calls and sampling complexity relative to classical Monte Carlo-based LSM.

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets quantum derivative pricing as its main finance application, noting that such algorithms depend heavily on basic arithmetic operations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, square root, exponentiation, and arcsine, and that inefficient implementations can inject substantial noise leading to inappropriate pricing outcomes and impede concrete runtime estimates. The authors operate in fixed‑point arithmetic for reversible function evaluation, decompose Toffoli gates into three generalized ternary CNOTs of depth three, and reuse previously proposed intermediate‑qutrit adders, extending the same paradigm to multipliers and more complex functions like square root, exponentiation, and arcsine within a path‑loading–based amplitude‑estimation pricing algorithm that uses Gaussian state preparation and a re‑parameterization method for path loading.

They provide explicit resource formulas (e.g., for multiplication and square root) and show on a basket-derivative benchmark that T-cost and T-depth drop to zero with an overall depth of 162 million, compared to substantially larger T-cost and depth in prior qubit-only designs. Under a Kraus-operator noise model, they claim significantly improved circuit robustness: their decomposition yields a higher success probability and lower idle-error contribution, including an illustrative case where for a circuit with Toffoli count 30, success probability is about 0.4 vs. 0.01 for prior decompositions, corresponding to roughly a 40% decrease in probability of error, and they also derive explicit truncation and discretization error bounds for the pricing algorithm.

The authors do not present new classical runtime or resource measurements themselves but use the classical Monte Carlo convergence rate as the conceptual baseline for the purported quantum speedup of the derivative-pricing algorithm they build upon.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that inefficient arithmetic blocks can introduce substantial noise, potentially yielding inappropriate derivative pricing outcomes, which motivates their focus on improving these subroutines. Regarding hardware, they recognize that adopting higher-dimensional (qutrit) gates increases the number of possible error channels—scaling as O(3^4) for a 3-level system—and explicitly treat this as a caveat even while arguing overall error reductions at the circuit level.

  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper suggests extending the intermediate‑qudit decomposition strategy beyond the specific arithmetic and derivative-pricing circuits studied here, proposing more detailed time-improvement estimates and the application of intermediate‑qudit decompositions to other quantum circuits as a direction for future research.

=== PAPER 674c681a57d0 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The report frames the problem as the heavy computational burden of pricing financial derivatives and computing risk measures such as Value at Risk (VaR), which commonly rely on Monte Carlo simulation and PDE solvers, and surveys quantum computing techniques that might accelerate these tasks, with a particular focus on developments since a prior NEASQC deliverable. It also notes a separate line of work that seeks to build quantum-inspired models of financial markets rather than just speeding up classical methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors review several gate-based quantum approaches: (i) quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC), which uses an oracle U to load the path probability distribution and a unitary V to encode the payoff, together with amplitude estimation schemes; (ii) quantum algorithms for PDE-based pricing that map option pricing PDEs to imaginary-time evolution under a Hermitian Hamiltonian and then simulate this evolution variationally on NISQ hardware; and (iii) other approaches such as quantum finance modelling based on a Merton–Schrödinger equation, quantum deep hedging via quantum reinforcement learning layers, and martingale pricing via quantum linear programming and density-operator-based “quantum assets.” All of these are discussed under an explicit NISQ-computing focus because of limits in qubit counts, circuit depth, and noise.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-011, C-030, C-031, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the algorithmic side, the report emphasizes that quantum amplitude estimation (AE) can in principle reduce the number of oracle calls compared to standard Monte Carlo, while parallel AE variants typically offer better depth control for NISQ devices. However, empirical and theoretical analyses cited in the report show that even low-strength noise can prevent achieving the quadratic speedup, with error saturating beyond a certain number of Grover applications, and that linear AE schedules tend to perform best under realistic noise. The report also highlights that approximate state loading may yield lower overall error than exact loading on noisy hardware, that engineered likelihood functions combined with Bayesian inference improve performance over conventional likelihoods, and that a variational PDE solver for option pricing can be implemented with poly(d·log(1/ε)) few-qubit gates on small quantum computers.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-017, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-028, C-034, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The report repeatedly benchmarks quantum proposals against classical Monte Carlo and PDE methods: Monte Carlo is described as the de facto industry standard because it is easy to implement, general, and scales well with dimension, while PDE solvers can converge faster in low-dimensional cases. Quantum amplitude estimation is presented as promising a quadratic reduction in required samples/oracle calls versus classical Monte Carlo in ideal conditions, and some PDE-based quantum solvers are said to potentially offer exponential speedups in very specific cases, though the authors stress that most of the observed performance improvements in recent work are only up to constant factors rather than changes in asymptotic scaling. They also caution that when realistic noise and error correction are taken into account, the effective speedup over classical methods may disappear for all practical instance sizes.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-019, C-041, C-043]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors enumerate multiple limitations. Hardware-wise, current NISQ devices suffer from limited qubit counts, restricted circuit depths, and significant noise, which motivates focusing on shallow, NISQ-compatible algorithms and leads to observations such as noise being the main limiting factor in AE experiments and the saturation of error improvements beyond a small number of Grover iterations. Methodologically, unitary-synthesis-based initialization is only applicable when the payoff evolution can be represented as a unitary, and initialization procedures must preserve relative phases—something that variational methods risk violating by introducing arbitrary phases. Both parallel and sequential MLAE approaches exhibit fundamental issues: depth limits on NISQ hardware stop error reduction beyond a certain point; critical points can make MLAE estimators biased and prevent further error reduction even without noise. For PDE-based quantum pricing, extracting a single amplitude in high-dimensional grids becomes a readout bottleneck that can eliminate any theoretical quantum advantage. Quantum deep hedging is constrained by the need for at least one qubit per time step and additional challenges when modelling rough paths. Finally, in a longer-term, fault-tolerant regime, the authors argue that the overhead of error correction may render quadratic speedups ineffective by pushing the problem sizes at which any speedup appears into an impractically large regime.
    [codes: C-005, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-032, C-037, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Looking ahead, the report suggests that near-term practical benefits from quantum computing in pricing and VaR may come less from speedups and more from reductions in energy consumption, implying an agenda of studying energy–accuracy trade-offs for quantum versus classical methods. The authors also implicitly point to further research on NISQ-friendly techniques such as approximate state loading, improved amplitude estimation under noise, and more efficient variational PDE solvers, though they do not lay out a detailed roadmap.
    [codes: C-017, C-021, C-033, C-034, C-044]

    [codes: C-006, C-011, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the review organizes QAMC work into three application blocks and dissects common subroutines such as initialization and amplitude estimation, giving particular attention to how different AE variants (parallel, sequential, generalized Grover, QSP-based) trade off depth, bias, and robustness to noise. In regression, convex portfolio optimization, spectral clustering, Bayesian inference, and various quantum ML models, the quantum methods are presented as enhancements to classical linear algebra or optimization routines rather than outright replacements, often assuming access models similar to those in classical oracle-based analyses. Hardware case studies compare quantum implementations to classical Monte Carlo or heuristic optimizers (e.g., genetic algorithms in portfolio optimization), framing any empirical advantage as problem- and instance-specific rather than universal.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The survey is explicit that practical quantum advantage in finance has not yet been demonstrated, emphasizing that current NISQ hardware is noisy, limited in circuit depth, constrained by qubit connectivity and gate-speed/fidelity tradeoffs, and therefore unable to solve real-life-scale financial problems more efficiently and accurately than classical systems. It underscores methodological limitations: variational and annealing approaches are fundamentally heuristic; many QLSA- and quantum-ML-based speedups rely on strong data-loading and oracle assumptions; nonlinear PDEs usually require linearization to fit QLSA; and path-dependent derivatives pose complexity for both classical and quantum pricing. The paper further notes that data movement between classical and quantum devices and efficient state preparation are critical bottlenecks; that some experiments, such as QAE-based risk analysis, cannot achieve practical advantage on NISQ devices; and that near-term HHL variants trade away formal asymptotic speedups for implementability. Collectively, the authors caution that hardware noise, limited qubit counts, heuristic performance guarantees, and stringent access assumptions materially constrain the current applicability of the surveyed methods.

More broadly, the survey points to further exploration of quantum generative models, quantum neural networks, and quantum-native NLP as fertile areas once hardware and data-access constraints are alleviated.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the survey is largely conceptual but anchors its discussion with selected hardware experiments on superconducting, annealing, and trapped-ion platforms, explicitly noting when algorithms are heuristic or when speedups are purely asymptotic and contingent on strong assumptions (e.g., efficient data access or oracular training data). === PAPER 6f039fcdad9d (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the task as solving ordinary and partial differential equations (DEs) using quantum computers, motivated by the importance of DEs across science and engineering and the desire to explore quantum potential for such problems. It benchmarks the proposed approach on a damped mass-spring system initial value problem over a fixed time interval and on a Poisson equation under multiple boundary-condition types.
    [codes: C-004, C-020, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a novel variational quantum algorithm (VQA) based on Lagrange polynomial encoding, offering two circuit architectures that trade off qubit count against gate count. The method is hybrid quantum–classical and tailored for NISQ devices, uses Hadamard-test–based derivative quantum circuits so that a single circuit yields expectation derivatives, and employs local cost functions (magnetization-based observables) to mitigate barren plateaus. Implementation details include encoding via a carefully scaled arccos feature map chosen for derivative stability, Chebyshev-node training points, two-part optimization with evolving training and regularization points, and explicit handling of initial/boundary conditions via function shifts and loss terms.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-005, C-007, C-009, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-024]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reports that its Hadamard-Lagrange VQA produces Lagrange-interpolating polynomial solutions that, on the damped mass-spring benchmark, appear of better quality and with more consistent optimization across random initializations than the Kyriienko-inspired comparator, while already being competitive in gate complexity. For the Poisson benchmark with periodic, Neumann, and Dirichlet boundary conditions, the proposed method matches the comparator’s loss after about 300 iterations but yields substantially lower mean absolute errors—4×, 3×, and 6× smaller—and better adherence to boundary conditions. Across both benchmarks the authors conclude that their two architectures reduce gate complexity while providing similar or better solution quality than existing VQAs.
    [codes: C-017, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not report any direct comparison to classical numerical solvers; all comparative results are against other quantum VQAs (Kyriienko-inspired Chebyshev encoding and the Sato et al. Poisson algorithm).
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-027, C-033, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that both their Hadamard-Lagrange algorithm and the Kyriienko-inspired baseline are meshless, polynomial-fitting approaches that require continuity in the problem definition, which constrains the class of DEs they can handle straightforwardly. They further note that encoding the variable with linear polynomials, as in their scheme, may be suboptimal for nonlinear problems, indicating that the present encoding may not generalize well to highly nonlinear DEs.
    [codes: C-037, C-038]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future work directions include assessing the performance of the proposed VQA in higher-dimensional settings and across a wider variety of differential equations, as well as extending the method to handle nonlinear DEs and testing it on quantum hardware.
    [codes: C-039, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is a novel VQA that uses Lagrange polynomial encoding combined with Hadamard-test differentiation to approximate DE solutions, offered in two circuit architectures that trade qubits for gates. The authors claim this design reduces gate complexity relative to prior VQAs while achieving similar or better solution quality on representative DE benchmarks.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-018, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper situates its VQA within hybrid quantum–classical schemes suited to near-term devices, explicitly addressing trainability via local cost functions to mitigate barren plateaus. It details boundary-condition enforcement using shifts and loss terms, uses Chebyshev nodes to choose training points in order to avoid the Runge phenomenon, and introduces regularization via partitioning point sets as a way to reduce algorithmic complexity. The Lagrange encoding angles are specifically chosen for derivative stability, and the optimization workflow follows and extends established iterative training procedures from prior work.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-019, C-021]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: None; all verified codes were incorporated into dimensions 1–8.
    [codes: —]

=== PAPER 75a7b04fa681 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the state-preparation or probability loading bottleneck in quantum Monte Carlo for financial applications, aiming to efficiently encode univariate and multivariate financial probability distributions into quantum states using tensor networks. It explicitly focuses on high-dimensional financial distributions from a bank as test cases, positioning the work within quantum Monte Carlo–based financial modeling where the theoretical quadratic speedup is threatened by costly state preparation. The goal is to obtain scalable, accurate encodings of these distributions suitable for QMC-based pricing and risk simulations.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-005, C-007, C-032, C-046]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a tensor-train (TT) representation of discretized probability distributions built via the TT-cross algorithm, then map this TT format directly to quantum gate sequences for amplitude encoding in QMC. They describe how tensor networks compress high-dimensional data and mitigate the curse of dimensionality, use specific quantization schemes (Sequential, Mirroring, Interleaving) to encode multivariate distributions into a TT, and then construct unitary operators from TT cores with an SVD-based iterative procedure under the assumption that TT bond dimensions are powers of two. Circuit depth is further reduced by merging compatible gates, and circuits are implemented in Qiskit using UnitaryGate and evaluated mainly through simulations, with hardware tests for a small univariate case.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-035, C-038, C-041, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Empirically, the TT-cross method is reported to achieve high-accuracy encodings of financial distributions, including a Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance of 7.2×10⁻⁵ for a univariate case with 16 qubits, and relatively low KL divergences (~10⁻² in the worst high-dimensional scenarios). The authors find that Mirroring quantization performs best for bivariate distributions and Interleaving is most effective for higher-dimensional multivariate cases, while TT-based circuits preserve equivalence to the original TT state even after depth-reduction by gate merging. They also report that TT-cross training time scales logarithmically with the number of discretization points, and that TT-based circuits exhibit linear circuit-depth scaling in the number of qubits, in contrast to the exponential depth growth observed for Qiskit’s built-in method.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-004, C-023, C-030, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Relative to classical and existing quantum-like baselines, the authors argue that Grover–Rudolph-style state preparation and Qiskit’s built-in log-normal loading scale poorly, with state-preparation complexity growing with the full number of discretization points and circuit depth increasing exponentially in qubits. In contrast, they claim that TT-cross–based probability loading mitigates the curse of dimensionality by yielding circuits with linear depth scaling and training routines whose complexity scales logarithmically with system size, thus improving circuit-depth scalability compared to traditional methods and making large circuits more practical.
    [codes: C-003, C-006, C-008, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that typical query-complexity-based speedup claims for QMC may substantially overstate practical advantage once full computational overheads, including state preparation, are considered, and that this overhead can negate the theoretical quadratic speedup. State preparation itself is identified as a major bottleneck, with the standard Grover–Rudolph method scaling poorly with precision, qGANs incurring long training times and heavy classical–quantum integration, and quantum-walk–based encoders being limited to discrete-value problems. Within their own TT-based scheme, the authors note that Sequential quantization fails to preserve multivariate correlations and leads to poor convergence, Mirroring is not straightforward to generalize beyond the bivariate setting, and univariate TT-cross approximations degrade in precision beyond about 15 qubits even when bond dimension is increased. They further report that hardware noise significantly distorts the encoded distribution on current devices, causing notably worse outcomes than noiseless simulations, which leads them to omit hardware tests for multivariate cases as they would not yield meaningful results.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-020, C-022, C-034, C-039, C-044, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose exploring alternative methods for approximating probability distributions in tensor-train format as a future research avenue. They also suggest leveraging analytical formulas of certain distributions to directly encode them into TT form, potentially bypassing some of the approximation overhead associated with TT-cross.
    [codes: C-049, C-050]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims that applying the TT-cross algorithm to the probability loading problem yields a particularly promising and scalable way to represent general probability distributions that can be efficiently expressed as quantum circuits for QMC, with circuit and operation complexity scaling logarithmically with system size and linear circuit-depth growth in practice. It further highlights as contributions the design and evaluation of three quantization schemes—Sequential, Mirroring, and Interleaving—for encoding multivariate financial distributions into tensor trains, with empirical identification of Mirroring as best for bivariate and Interleaving as best for higher-dimensional cases.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-013, C-015, C-017, C-021, C-023, C-046, C-048]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the authors emphasize that TT-cross training and TT-to-circuit mapping are conducted entirely on classical machines with stated guarantees for convergence and complexity, enabling scalable circuit construction. They describe using real univariate and multivariate financial distributions supplied by Itaú Unibanco, discretizing and binary-encoding them into TT format, and implementing the resulting circuits in Qiskit 0.45.0 via UnitaryGate. Evaluation relies on standard distance measures such as Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance and KL divergence, along with circuit-depth and training-time scaling analyses, and includes a small-scale real-hardware test that exposes the impact of noise; however, for multivariate settings the study is confined to simulations to maintain a controlled environment and isolate tensor-network algorithmic effects.
    [codes: C-012, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-035, C-036, C-038, C-040, C-042, C-043, C-039, C-044, C-045]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Tensor networks in general are described as enabling compression of high-dimensional datasets, significantly reducing computational complexity and memory requirements beyond the specific application to QMC. This broader motivation underpins the choice of TT-cross for probability loading but extends to other potential high-dimensional financial modeling tasks.
    [codes: C-014]

=== PAPER 79a526ef5902 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames a methodological problem: rapidly growing complexity and diversity of quantum compilation frameworks makes it hard to understand and compare their optimization behavior, especially for NISQ-oriented applications. The authors argue that there is a need for a dedicated, systematic cross-benchmarking tool to study how different sequences of optimization passes and subroutines interact and affect circuit metrics across compilation stages.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-010, C-011]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work introduces Arline Benchmarks, an open-source platform that configures benchmarking experiments via JSONNet files defining three components: target circuits, quantum hardware models, and a compilation pipeline. The platform allows users to build custom pipelines that mix optimization and routing routines from different vendors, track circuit metrics at each compilation stage, and use hardware-aware cost functions based on two-qubit counts/depth and average log-fidelity. Benchmarks use both randomly generated circuits parameterized by two-qubit gate density and structured algorithmic circuits, and the platform also supports constructing composite pipelines that chain heterogeneous subroutines in a single stack.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-047, C-053]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: Across KAK-based two-qubit benchmarks, the authors find that Qiskit, Pytket, and Cirq compress random circuits to theoretically optimal CX and single-qubit counts, whereas PyZX fails to reach this optimum. For three-qubit circuits, Pytket achieves the best compression relative to theoretical bounds, while Cirq performs worst. Routing benchmarks show Qiskit and Pytket having similar overheads over a range of connectivities, with Qiskit outperforming Pytket on dense graphs and Cirq incurring the largest routing overheads. On random circuits with low CX density, compilers significantly reduce single-qubit and total gate count but PyZX can even double the CX count; for high CX density, CX reduction is modest, while PyZX excels on phase-polynomial circuits. For structured algorithms, compression performance is consistent within a circuit class: ChemPass dominates for Trotterized dynamics depth and CX depth, and PyZX and ChemPass show similar performance for UCCSD circuits; domain-specific ranking of subroutines reveals that PytketChem and FullReduce are strongest for chemistry, while some passes like MergeInteractions can worsen cost. Hardware-specific studies indicate that constrained-connectivity devices (except certain all-to-all or trapped-ion architectures) attain similar best two-qubit compression, but rebasing to IonQ and Rigetti gate sets leads to notably worse single-qubit metrics. A key high-level result is that composite pipelines, where pass order is carefully chosen, can achieve additional circuit compression beyond the best individual subroutine and even surpass expert-designed pipelines.
    [codes: C-004, C-007, C-014, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-046, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper’s comparisons are primarily between different quantum compiler frameworks and subroutines rather than against purely classical optimization methods; it positions Arline Benchmarks as analogous to MLPerf in machine learning, providing standardized metrics and tests for this cross-compiler comparison. Within this quantum–software landscape, the authors compare vendor pipelines (Qiskit, Pytket, Cirq) and specialized optimizers (PyZX, ChemPass, FullReduce, MergeInteractions), highlighting relative strengths and weaknesses in gate-count compression, depth reduction, and hardware-aware cost across random, structured, and hardware-constrained settings.
    [codes: C-004, C-013, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-042, C-043, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-054]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that understanding compiler optimization performance is intrinsically difficult because it is hard to predict the effect of particular sequences of passes, and that benchmarking must therefore rely on a wide variety of carefully designed tests and metrics. They caution that single-qubit gate metrics are especially sensitive to the chosen input/output gate sets and must be interpreted carefully, and they explicitly describe their hardware-aware cost model as "quite simplistic." They also note the absence of a simple predictor for compression potential of given frameworks on structured circuits, and emphasize that the search space for composite pipelines grows factorially with the number of subroutines and stages, making exhaustive exploration infeasible.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-021, C-023, C-044, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper proposes replacing handcrafted cost functions with neural-network-based approximators that could better capture hardware-specific performance characteristics. The authors also plan to expand Arline Benchmarks by supporting more compiler frameworks and by enlarging the database of target circuits and metrics, explicitly mentioning additions such as T gate counts and quantum volume for compressed circuits.
    [codes: C-024, C-056, C-057]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim as their main contribution an open-source platform, Arline Benchmarks, that automates benchmarking of quantum compilers for NISQ applications, including stage-by-stage metric analysis and visualization. They further introduce the concept of composite compilation pipelines that combine compiler-specific optimization routines from multiple providers into a single stack, and show that such composite pipelines can discover more efficient pass sequences and achieve additional circuit compression beyond individual vendor compilers and expert-designed pipelines. They argue that the toolkit enables researchers and developers to gain new insights into compiler characteristics that were previously difficult to obtain.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-005, C-008, C-009, C-014, C-015, C-019, C-054, C-055]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the framework enforces experiment specification through JSONNet configuration files that clearly separate target circuits, hardware models, and compilation pipelines, supporting reproducibility and systematic variation. The platform tracks detailed circuit metrics, including a formally defined compression factor for different gate classes and a hardware-aware cost function that penalizes circuit depth and two-qubit gate infidelities, and it visualizes how these metrics evolve through each compilation stage. Benchmark workloads include both random circuits—motivated as a practical choice for compiler and hardware testing and parameterized via two-qubit gate density—and a diverse set of structured quantum algorithms, enabling analysis of performance consistency within circuit classes and across hardware-specific rebasing steps.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-025, C-026, C-041, C-047]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper situates the need for standardized benchmarking in analogy with the MLPerf project from machine learning, using this comparison to motivate community-wide benchmarks for quantum compilers.
    [codes: C-013]
[SILO OVERLAY]
  SILO_RELEVANCE: This paper matters for derivative_pricing because it benchmarks quantum compilation workflows that would sit underneath pricing and Greeks circuits, where circuit depth, two-qubit count, and hardware-aware fidelity directly affect the practicality of running option-pricing workloads. Its strongest relevance is the evidence that pass ordering and composite pipelines can materially improve compression, which is important when derivative-pricing circuits must be made as shallow and hardware-efficient as possible.
    [silo_relevance_score: medium]
  KEY_POINT 1: Stage-by-stage benchmarking and metric tracking are directly useful for pricing/Greeks circuit optimization.
    [codes: C-005, C-015, C-016, C-022  dim_source: dimension_8]
  KEY_POINT 2: Custom pipelines that mix vendor subroutines can find better compression than any single compiler.
    [codes: C-008, C-019, C-054, C-055  dim_source: dimension_7]

[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames quantum computing as an evolutionary computing paradigm aimed at addressing complex, data- and computation-intensive problems in financial services, particularly in banking, insurance, high-frequency trading, and fraud/risk management. It formulates finance problems mainly as constrained and uncertain optimization, targeting three application groups: targeting and prediction (personalized services, fraud detection), trading optimization (portfolio rebalancing, derivatives valuation), and risk profiling (scenario simulations under regulatory pressure).
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-046, C-053, C-054, C-061, C-067, C-081]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The paper does not specify concrete quantum algorithms but conceptually describes quantum computation using qubits, superposition, and entanglement, emphasizing that quantum algorithms can avoid exhaustive sequential search and tackle combinatorial optimization. It discusses quantum logic gates, entangling gates, and system-level characteristics such as coherence time, connectivity, gate fidelity, and logical (error-corrected) qubits as key elements in realizing useful financial applications, and it notes superconducting and trapped-ion/atom-based qubits as primary hardware approaches.
    [codes: C-002, C-007, C-009, C-011, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-033, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-045, C-065]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: As a conceptual review, the paper reports no experimental or quantitative quantum results; instead it presents speculative performance claims. It asserts that entanglement and superposition can yield much higher speed and lower energy use than classical computers, that several computational issues could be solved more efficiently with quantum algorithms, and that as few as ~50 high-quality qubits could run certain algorithms in minutes. In finance, the authors claim that quantum computing could enlarge solution spaces beyond supercomputers, nearly double "power" with each added qubit, improve pattern discovery for targeting and prediction, enhance portfolio diversification and rebalancing, streamline settlement, accelerate and improve risk simulations, and improve investment gains, reduce capital needs, create new investment opportunities, and strengthen fraud, risk, and compliance management.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-014, C-018, C-028, C-030, C-037, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-060, C-065, C-066, C-070, C-071, C-072, C-073, C-074, C-080, C-081]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors contrast quantum and classical computing primarily at a conceptual level, arguing that classical machines encode information strictly in 0/1 bits, which restricts their ability and leads to intractability for certain combinatorial problems, whereas qubits can exist in multiple states simultaneously and be entangled. They claim quantum computers process data differently, excel at complex simulations and data analysis, and have solution spaces orders of magnitude larger than even supercomputers, while also emphasizing that everyday office applications may not see speedups. They further contend that some problems may never be solvable by traditional computers regardless of time, highlighting combinatorial growth of variables as a bottleneck that quantum approaches can mitigate by not testing all solutions sequentially.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-049]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges multiple limitations and caveats. On hardware, it notes that quantum computers are difficult and expensive to manufacture, require ultra-cold environments, and involve fragile quantum states where even minor disturbances cause decoherence and destroy computation; all operations must complete before decoherence, and gate errors accumulate quickly, so low gate fidelity and limited gate depth can render large qubit counts relatively useless. Architecturally, superconducting systems are constrained by physical adjacency of qubits, and identical qubits plus sufficient fidelity (roughly enabling n×n gates for n qubits) are needed for useful computation. Application-wise, the authors explicitly state that quantum computing will not speed up routine applications such as Word or Excel, that real-time behavioral analytics and accurate fraud detection are currently difficult with existing systems (e.g., high false positives, slow onboarding), and that Monte Carlo-based risk models are constrained by error scaling. At the strategic level, they admit that commercial adoption may take several years and explicitly concede that there is no clear timeline for when quantum computing will realize its full potential or whether it will achieve all the proposed financial and real-world functions.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-021, C-022, C-027, C-031, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-041, C-042, C-044, C-056, C-057, C-059, C-063, C-064, C-068, C-082]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors situate quantum computing as a longer-term opportunity, suggesting that widespread commercial applications in finance may take several years and that future regulation will likely increase compliance costs, strengthening the case for more powerful risk tools. They highlight the combination of quantum and cloud computing as a way to expand accessible applications and foresee quantum manufacturers using quantum computers themselves to discover improved algorithms and qubit technologies. More broadly, they speculate on future uses in drug discovery, climate-change mitigation, and logistics optimization as areas where further research and development could unfold.
    [codes: C-051, C-069, C-075, C-079, C-076, C-077, C-078]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its contribution as a conceptual exposition of how quantum computing—grounded in superposition, entanglement, and improved hardware metrics—could transform financial services across targeting and prediction, trading optimization, and risk profiling, particularly for high-frequency trading and fraud detection. It emphasizes the idea that quantum computing’s enlarged solution space and combinatorial optimization capabilities can unlock new arbitrage opportunities, enhance personalization, and restructure operational processes in ways classical computing cannot.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-046, C-047, C-048, C-049, C-050, C-052, C-060, C-065, C-070, C-071, C-072, C-073, C-074, C-080, C-081]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: The article is a high-level conceptual and review-style piece with no implemented quantum algorithms, datasets, or experiments, and thus offers no reproducible methodology or empirical evaluation. Its most technical elements concern system-assessment concepts—such as analyzing qubits alongside system-level qualities (connectivity, coherence, quality), defining coherence time, connectivity, gate fidelity, and error-corrected logical qubits, and arguing that qubit count alone is an inadequate power metric—rather than concrete financial modeling protocols. All reported numbers (e.g., qubit thresholds, fraud false-positive rates, revenue loss estimates) are cited or asserted rather than derived from original experiments presented in the paper.

=== PAPER 7e0bccd34042 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the problem of derivatives valuation, specifically option pricing, by framing it as the computation of expectations that reduce to evaluating integrals over the underlying asset’s distribution. The authors formulate pricing either via Fourier series of the probability density function (PDF) or of the cumulative distribution function (CDF), so that the integral becomes a sum over products of Fourier coefficients associated with the distribution and the payoff. They design three approaches around this Fourier-based distribution estimation framework to address the option pricing task.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-014, C-015, C-018, C-022]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work proposes two hybrid classical–quantum methods based on parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs) acting as trainable function approximators whose output functions admit a Fourier series representation with a frequency spectrum determined by the encoding Hamiltonians. In Method I (supervised), a PQC is trained on labeled data to approximate the PDF and its derivative in an H1-type risk, and Fourier coefficients of the learned function are extracted from direct circuit evaluations using a discrete Fourier transform. In Method II (self-supervised), a PQC is trained to approximate the CDF using only samples and an empirical CDF with additional boundary/endpoint constraint terms, again leveraging PQCs’ expressivity and Fourier-structured output to recover CDF-based Fourier coefficients. A third, benchmark method (Method III) uses Quantum Accelerated Monte Carlo via a modified Real Quantum Amplitude Estimation (mRQAE) procedure that embeds the integral into a quantum amplitude and estimates Fourier coefficients, including their sign, by repeated circuit executions.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The numerical experiments indicate that the proposed PQC-based methods achieve what the authors describe as “remarkable accuracy” and are presented as a competitive quantum alternative for derivatives valuation. For the QAMC-based benchmark, the authors recall that amplitude-estimation-based Monte Carlo achieves a quadratic improvement in the number of queries needed for a given mean squared error compared to classical Monte Carlo. Empirically, they observe that Method II, which learns the CDF from samples, can reach option pricing accuracy comparable to the QAMC benchmark while using only about 10,000 data samples, whereas Method III (QAMC) requires on the order of 5,000 shots per Fourier coefficient for high accuracy, implying hundreds of thousands of shots overall. They also report that intermediate PQC circuit sizes give the best performance for Methods I and II, and that increasing the number of Fourier coefficients improves the accuracy of the QAMC-based Method III, especially at lower shot counts. Training the quantum models on a wider interval than the target evaluation range is found to reduce Gibbs phenomena and yield smoother Fourier reconstructions, improving numerical behavior.
    [codes: C-005, C-013, C-018, C-027, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical Monte Carlo serves as an implicit baseline through the use of Quantum Accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC), which the authors state offers a quadratic improvement in query complexity, in mean squared error, over its classical Monte Carlo counterpart. Within the quantum approaches, QAMC (Method III) is explicitly used as a benchmark to quantitatively assess the proposed PQC-based models in terms of computational cost and accuracy of Fourier coefficient extraction, and the authors report that Method II achieves similar accuracy with fewer data samples than QAMC needs shots per coefficient. The paper positions the PQC-based methods as competitive quantum alternatives rather than providing a detailed head‑to‑head comparison against purely classical Fourier-based or machine-learning-based pricing schemes.
    [codes: C-004, C-007, C-013, C-028, C-030, C-035, C-036, C-039]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that their Fourier-based PDF approach relies on truncating the density to a finite interval [a, b], assuming this does not significantly degrade accuracy, which may not hold for all asset distributions or payoffs. They note that Gibbs phenomena can arise in Fourier reconstructions on the target interval, necessitating training on an enlarged interval to mitigate oscillations, implicitly highlighting sensitivity to boundary effects. In the conclusions, they emphasize that variability and uncertainty in their numerical experiments suggest the need for multiple experimental runs and statistical post-analysis to disentangle different sources of error, indicating concerns about robustness and noise in the estimations.
    [codes: C-016, C-026, C-027, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper implies that future work should include more systematic statistical analysis across multiple experimental runs to better isolate uncertainty sources in the quantum pricing pipeline and to characterize the stability of the methods. The acknowledged need for interval truncation and mitigation of Gibbs phenomena also suggests that further investigation into adaptive domain selection and improved boundary handling for Fourier-based quantum models would be a natural extension.
    [codes: C-016, C-026, C-027, C-040]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim novelty in introducing two hybrid classical–quantum methods for option pricing that reconstruct Fourier series representations of the underlying statistical distributions directly from PQC-based quantum machine learning models. They further highlight that the frequency spectrum of the learned quantum model is explicitly controlled by the encoding Hamiltonians, leveraging universal-approximation-style results for PQCs on function spaces, and that they explore both PDF-based and CDF-based Fourier representations, with the CDF route motivated by smoother behavior and more stable numerical approximations. The study also emphasizes the design of three approaches—including a QAMC-based mRQAE benchmark—to systematically compare cost and accuracy for Fourier-coefficient extraction in derivatives valuation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-008, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-019, C-022, C-028, C-030]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper grounds its quantum models in prior work on PQCs as universal function approximators over spaces of continuous, Lp, and Sobolev functions, and exploits the fact that PQC outputs can be written as Fourier series with spectra fixed by the encoding Hamiltonians. For training, they define an H1-based empirical risk that incorporates derivative information, and for the CDF-based self-supervised method they add endpoint or boundary constraint terms to stabilize the fit using only samples and empirical CDFs. The authors take care to reduce Gibbs phenomena by training over an enlarged interval and then evaluating on a narrower one, and they derive analytic Fourier coefficients for payoffs so that pricing reduces to sums over products of distribution and payoff coefficients. Their experimental design includes examining the impact of data-set size and PQC dimensionality on performance and using QAMC as a benchmark for cost and accuracy; however, all implementations run on simulators and the paper itself recommends multiple runs plus statistical post-analysis to properly characterize uncertainty, indicating an awareness of variability and reproducibility concerns.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-040]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: Several codes elaborate on specific algebraic or design insights within the proposed framework: the transformation of integrals of products into sums over products of Fourier coefficients simplifies pricing computations; using the CDF is argued to handle discontinuities in PDFs more stably; and the mRQAE variant is chosen specifically because it can recover both magnitude and sign of Fourier coefficients, which is crucial for accurate reconstruction. The observation that Method II avoids explicit knowledge of the PDF and operates only on samples is emphasized as a practical benefit in realistic derivative-pricing settings where the exact density is not available.
    [codes: C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-029, C-034]

=== PAPER 82475e54c193 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the challenge of representing and analyzing continuous-time stochastic processes (CTSPs) on a quantum computer, motivated by the fact that analytic solutions are often unavailable and classical Monte Carlo for such processes can be very resource-intensive. It explicitly focuses on overcoming two core bottlenecks for financial and actuarial applications: efficient quantum storage of entire sample paths (crucial for path-dependent problems in financial engineering, quantitative trading, and actuarial science) and efficient extraction of history-sensitive quantities such as weighted path integrals and first-hitting times. The framework is positioned as broadly applicable to CTSPs in finance, including option pricing under jump-diffusion models and ruin probabilities in collective risk models.
    [codes: C-001, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-014, C-015, C-039, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a quantum framework for continuous-time stochastic processes (QCTSP) with a two-stage workflow: data preparation (encoding and compression of paths) followed by information extraction. They introduce two quantum representations for general QCTSPs and corresponding state-preparation circuits that exploit a holding-time observation to reduce qubit count, circuit depth, and gate complexity, including specialized constructions for Lévy, Poisson, compound Poisson, continuous Markov, and Cox processes. For information extraction, they design methods to evaluate weightless and time-weighted integrals via summations of directed areas and to extract history-sensitive information using sequences of flag qubits; the prepared QCTSP states are designed to be usable as submodules in other quantum algorithms, do not rely on qRAM or oracles, and can be parallelized via equivalence-class decompositions with relatively mild connectivity/topological requirements.
    [codes: C-002, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-036, C-041, C-042, C-005, C-034, C-035, C-032, C-033, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors claim that their data-preparation scheme encodes and compresses CTSP information with significant space and time savings, including an exponential reduction in resources with respect to a key feature parameter, identified as the average holding time τ_avg. They report that for many standard process families (Lévy, Poisson, compound Poisson, continuous Markov, Cox) their circuits achieve explicit asymptotic resource bounds, such as preparing a Lévy process on n log(nS) qubits with O(S + n log(nS)) depth, and that memoryless holding times can be prepared with logarithmic qubit counts and constant depth. On the analysis side, they extend quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo, claiming quadratic acceleration in decoding and processing compressed information relative to classical Monte Carlo, while also demonstrating that their QCTSP-based option pricing under the Merton jump–diffusion model matches the Merton formula and that their ruin-probability application constitutes a first introduction of quantum computing into insurance mathematics. They also summarize that overall preparation complexity is governed by time horizon T and memory length, and that their method reduces the number of copies of the state space from O(T) to O(n ln τ_avg).
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-006, C-038, C-022, C-023]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The framework is explicitly positioned against classical numerical methods, with the authors noting that conventional Monte Carlo simulations for CTSPs demand large storage and computational resources. They claim that their information-extraction stage offers a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo methods, effectively extending quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo to continuous time, and that the QCTSP preparation subroutine can help alleviate the classical data-loading bottleneck common in other quantum algorithms. For the Merton jump–diffusion application, they state that the simulated quantum results are consistent with the classical Merton formula, and they emphasize that their approach avoids certain classical-style input assumptions by not requiring qRAM or oracle-based access.
    [codes: C-010, C-003, C-004, C-006, C-038, C-005, C-022, C-040]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that prior quantum work has not fully solved CTSP state preparation—particularly lacking in full-path storage needed for many financial engineering and quantitative trading tasks—and they position their work as addressing but not exhausting these issues. They explicitly state that their article lacks a detailed and quantitative analysis of hardware efficiency and implementation aspects. They also recognize that they have not developed preparation schemes for several financially relevant CTSPs such as Hawkes processes and that their current treatment of path-dependent information extraction is incomplete, calling for more techniques to handle such quantities. Finally, they note that topics like quantum walks and their application to finance are outside the scope of the current work.
    [codes: C-013, C-014, C-015, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper outlines several directions for future research: performing more detailed and quantitative analyses of hardware efficiency and architectural constraints; extending the QCTSP preparation framework to other financially relevant CTSPs such as Hawkes processes; exploring additional application domains including high-frequency trading, actuarial science, and further option-pricing settings; and developing more advanced techniques for efficient extraction of path-dependent information. The authors also point to quantum walks and their application in finance as an area they have not yet explored.
    [codes: C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors present their work as an algorithmic framework for quantum continuous-time stochastic processes that simultaneously addresses efficient state preparation and information extraction, asserting exponential reductions in key resource parameters and a quadratic acceleration over classical Monte Carlo, and highlighting that the resulting prepared states can serve as generic input submodules for other quantum algorithms without relying on qRAM. They emphasize the versatility of the framework across multiple domains including finance and statistics, and they claim novelty in two showcased financial applications: handling discontinuous price movements in Merton jump–diffusion option pricing and providing, to their knowledge, the first quantum-computing-based treatment of ruin probability in insurance mathematics.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-017, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-038, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the framework is structured into a clear two-stage process (data preparation and information extraction), with complexity analyses that tie resource requirements to time horizon and memory length and provide explicit asymptotic bounds for several standard CTSP families. The authors design circuits that avoid qRAM and are intended to be implementable on hardware with comparatively low connectivity and topological constraints, and they mention possibilities for parallel preparation based on equivalence-class decompositions of the sample space. However, they explicitly concede that a detailed quantitative hardware-efficiency analysis is missing, indicating that their resource claims are primarily asymptotic and theoretical rather than empirically benchmarked on specific devices.
    [codes: C-002, C-018, C-019, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper notes that the complexity of state preparation increases with the memory length of the process and that for memoryless processes the holding times follow exponential distributions that enable constant-depth preparation, providing theoretical characterization of how process memory affects quantum circuit design.

=== PAPER 8273c874208a (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses derivative pricing under the standard risk‑neutral framework, where the contract value is the discounted expectation of its payoff under the risk‑neutral measure, and focuses on Monte Carlo–style simulation for such expectations. It specifically targets cases where the derivative payoff (and thus price) can be negative, which breaks standard quantum Monte Carlo pipelines based on naive square‑root amplitude encoding.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-013, C-024]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose an alternative quantum pipeline that combines a direct encoding of the payoff (without square roots) into amplitudes with a modified Robust Quantum Amplitude Estimation (mRQAE) routine that can read all information in the quantum state, including the sign. To make implementation tractable, they restrict to models admitting exact single‑step simulation (specifically the Black–Scholes SDE under the risk‑neutral measure) so that the terminal underlying can be encoded in one step, and they present explicit pseudocode for mRQAE along with oracle/state‑preparation constructions.
    [codes: C-002, C-003, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-016, C-018, C-021, C-027]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper reiterates that Quantum Accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) offers a quadratic improvement in sampling error over classical Monte Carlo and shows that, in emulator tests, the proposed alternative pipeline retains these asymptotic speedups. It demonstrates that naive square‑root encoding fails to converge for negative‑payoff contracts, while the combined direct‑encoding + mRQAE pipeline can recover the true negative prices (including for a cliquet option) without auxiliary mechanisms, and that mRQAE is asymptotically more efficient than RQAE and empirically competitive with mIQAE on both negative‑ and positive‑payoff contracts.
    [codes: C-004, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-013, C-019, C-020, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-028]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical Monte Carlo is used as the complexity and convergence baseline, with its statistical error scaling as O(1/√NC) compared to the quadratic improvement claimed for QAMC, and this contrast is explicitly discussed. The authors frame their results in terms of retaining this quadratic speedup relative to classical Monte Carlo while avoiding payoff splitting, but detailed empirical side‑by‑side runtime or error tables versus classical Monte Carlo are not reported.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-004]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors repeatedly emphasize that current quantum hardware is a major barrier to practical deployment of their pipeline: implementing the required oracle US demands an excessively large number of qubits, the Grover‑like routines necessary for amplitude amplification entail circuit depths incompatible with present‑day decoherence times, and the aggregate gate count would require gate error rates beyond current technological capabilities. They therefore work entirely in a simplified emulator setting (including exact simulation and reduced time stepping) and explicitly note that even with their algorithmic refinements, many practical issues remain unresolved under state‑of‑the‑art hardware constraints. They also acknowledge that direct encoding alone only partially solves the sign‑recovery problem and requires coupling with mRQAE.
    [codes: C-009, C-017, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Future research directions identified by the authors include developing more efficient state‑initialization schemes that approximately encode the target probability distributions, exploring alternative payoff encodings and normalizations that might reduce truncation effects, and systematically tuning or redesigning the parameter choices within mRQAE to improve efficiency, for example in terms of the total number of shots required.
    [codes: C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper claims novelty in presenting an alternative option‑pricing pipeline to standard QAMC that can handle derivatives with negative payoffs without decomposing the payoff into positive and negative parts. This is achieved by combining a direct encoding protocol that embeds sign information into the quantum state with the mRQAE algorithm to extract both magnitude and sign, thereby avoiding the usual splitting into separate codomains.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-018, C-027, C-028]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is implemented on a classical quantum emulator (Finisterrae III infrastructure at CESGA) rather than real hardware, and the authors provide schematic pseudocode for mRQAE and describe their experimental platform. They clearly document the simplifications adopted—such as restricting to Black–Scholes dynamics with exact single‑step simulation to avoid time discretization—as well as the benchmark setup comparing multiple amplitude estimation variants by oracle‑call counts, which supports reproducibility of the algorithmic evaluation.

=== PAPER 858a41cdb5b2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as designing quantum algorithms that can efficiently handle and manipulate arrays (including matrix-like data structures) by directly embedding their entries into quantum amplitudes, and providing an end-to-end pipeline from data loading through arithmetic manipulation to information extraction that can support such array-based tasks. The authors argue that direct amplitude embedding simplifies subsequent algebraic operations on the stored information compared with register-based encodings.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-004, C-007, C-008, C-009]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The proposed method is a direct amplitude-embedding framework where array entries f(i,j) are stored as amplitudes c_ij of a two-register 'quantum matrix' state, with indices i and j representing rows and columns respectively, and arithmetic is performed directly on these amplitudes without square-root encodings or register-based value representations. The pipeline is modularized into separate stages for data loading (including pointwise loading under an efficient-oracle assumption and specialized constant-array loading), an arithmetic toolkit on arrays (reversal, permutations, pairwise sums, reductions, scalar and array multiplication, scalar products), and information extraction via a Quantum Coin amplitude-estimation scheme enhanced by an iterative Grover-style zoom-in procedure and amplitude shifts over confidence intervals. Specific gate-level mechanisms include masking and controlled-X for row reversal, pivot-based recursive multi-controlled-X permutations and cyclic permutations with added controls, Hadamard-based pairwise addition and Walsh–Hadamard reductions, controlled rotations for multiplication by constants within [0,1], array multiplication with products encoded in specific ancilla branches, and composition of array products with reductions to obtain scalar products.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-005, C-007, C-008, C-010, C-013, C-016, C-018, C-019, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that state-of-the-art generic n‑qubit state preparation requires a number of CNOT gates scaling as 2^{n+1}, motivating their search for more efficient loading in structured cases such as constant arrays. For constant arrays, they state that their loading procedure uses, in the worst case, n_I X-gates, two Y-rotations, and a single multi-controlled NOT, and from this they infer that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed on a quantum computer to load a constant array than in the generic case. Within the arithmetic layer, they quantify that whole-matrix reversal can be more efficient than row- or column-only reversal, that reductions place row sums into the first column, and that array multiplication encodes the product of two arrays in the joint |0⟩ ancilla branch, which can then be combined with reductions to yield scalar products. For readout, they show that their Quantum Coin method with amplitude shift and iterative Grover amplification increases the measurement probability of the target basis state according to the standard amplification relation, effectively boosting the success probability within a specified confidence interval.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-020, C-027, C-031, C-032, C-036]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper primarily contrasts quantum vs. quantum approaches to state preparation, noting that existing generic loading techniques require exponentially many CNOTs in the number of qubits, whereas their constant-array loading uses only a number of gates scaling with the number of row qubits and a single multi-controlled NOT. On this basis, they claim that, in principle, exponentially fewer operations are needed to load constant arrays on a quantum computer, though the detailed comparison to classical loading costs is not elaborated beyond this asymptotic statement.
    [codes: C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations and conditional assumptions. They state that pointwise loading of generic arrays is 'generically not efficient', underscoring that their loading advantages are restricted to structured cases such as constant arrays and that the overall efficiency of their array multiplication procedure is tied to the efficiency of the underlying loading process. They explicitly assume the existence of a suitable efficient oracle for data loading, without which the end-to-end scheme would not be efficient. They also note that multiplication by a constant via controlled rotations is initially restricted to numbers between 0 and 1. At the operation level, they point out that swaps of two entries in an array are demanding operations, reflecting a cost overhead for fine-grained permutations. For their approximation of linear shifts via step functions, they caution that the method becomes inefficient if the required precision scales as 1/N in the number of discretisation points, indicating unfavorable scaling for high-accuracy piecewise approximations.
    [codes: C-011, C-012, C-021, C-029, C-030, C-040]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The provided codes do not report explicit statements about future research directions or proposed extensions beyond the presented framework and examples.
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions its novelty in offering a general-purpose framework for quantum algorithms that operate on arrays via direct embedding into amplitudes, thereby avoiding square roots and register encodings and, according to the authors, enabling simpler handling and combination of stored information. They highlight the modularization of the quantum algorithm pipeline into data loading, arithmetic manipulations, and read-out, and the construction of an efficient toolkit of quantum arithmetic operations on arrays, including explicit examples on manipulating generic oracles such as constant shifts and step-function approximations to linear shifts. They further claim that for constant arrays this framework can, in principle, achieve an exponential reduction in the number of operations required for loading compared with generic state-preparation methods.
