  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors consistently position quantum ML approaches relative to classical baselines, usually in terms of asymptotic complexity rather than realized empirical gains. They stress that no end-to-end quantum ML application with exponential speedup over a full classical workflow is currently known, and that even where subroutines offer exponential or quadratic advantages, data loading and readout can erode these benefits. In regression and clustering, they note the existence of quantum-inspired classical algorithms whose performance can rival or narrow the practical gap with quantum counterparts. For specific tasks like S&P 500 prediction, they report classical LSTM performance metrics and then suggest that quantum models such as PQCs or quantum LSTMs might improve expressivity and training complexity, without claiming demonstrated superiority. The paper also emphasizes that some quantum schemes, like the nearest-centroid hardware demo, do not presently claim any advantage in time complexity over classical methods.

  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper is explicit about multiple limitations. At a foundational level, it notes that efficient loading of classical data into quantum states and reading out classical outputs remains an open challenge, and that many linear-algebraic quantum routines cannot be applied "out of the box" to financial problems without stringent conditions and problem-specific customization. The authors emphasize that no complete quantum ML application with proven end-to-end exponential speedup over classical methods has been discovered, and highlight readout bottlenecks such as the need for O(d) copies of an output state to reconstruct regression outputs. They also acknowledge that some demonstrated methods, like the quantum nearest-centroid classifier, do not yield any time-complexity speedup and thus remain mainly proof-of-concept. Hardware and NISQ-era constraints are underlined, for instance in kernel estimation for QSVMs where the more asymptotically efficient technique is less feasible on noisy devices, and in clustering where large-scale q-means requires coreset strategies to be run on NISQ machines. On the algorithmic side, they flag barren plateaus as a serious obstacle for training variational quantum classifiers and wider VQC-based models. In reinforcement learning, they note that quantum RL schemes have not yet been directly applied to central financial use cases like automated trading. Overall, the review repeatedly tempers theoretical speedup claims with practical concerns about scalability, noise, and I/O overheads.

  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors identify several avenues for future work. They propose exploring PQC-based and potentially quantum LSTM-style models for asset pricing and time-series forecasting, hypothesizing advantages in expressivity and training despite the lack of current deployments. They suggest extending differentially private quantum Lasso-like methods for sparse regression in trend-following strategies and further developing adaptive variational algorithms, such as EVQE, to mitigate barren plateaus in VQCs. In clustering and feature extraction, they recommend developing coreset and QUBO-based schemes compatible with NISQ hardware, building on early successes like quantum-annealer-based credit-feature reduction. For reinforcement learning, they call out algorithmic trading and market making as promising but as-yet unexplored domains for direct quantum RL application. At a higher level, the conclusion positions the paper itself as a roadmap toward enriching finance with quantum ML techniques in the NISQ era and beyond, implicitly inviting systematic implementation, benchmarking, and integration of the surveyed methods.

=== PAPER ce2db00aac7a (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets credit valuation adjustment (CVA) as a quantum use case, motivated by the need to speed up statistical sampling tasks that today are handled by Monte Carlo simulation of stochastic exposure paths under regulatory requirements. CVA is formulated as an expectation over exposure, default probability, and discounting, and then decomposed into a bracketed term that can be expressed as a quantum expectation value of a projector on a suitable state. To make this amenable to quantum encoding, the authors discretize both time and asset prices and, in their benchmark, instantiate CVA for a single-asset European call option under geometric Brownian motion.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-023]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a two-step quantum workflow: (1) generate a circuit that prepares the joint distribution over time and price and encodes payoff, default and discount factors via controlled rotations; (2) apply a quantum amplitude-estimation routine—specifically, a Bayesian Engineered Likelihood Function (ELF) scheme designed to adapt to available quantum resources. Circuit generation itself is split into state preparation and controlled-rotation subroutines, with state preparation implemented either via a Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM) or a Matrix Product State (MPS) trained to approximate the target distribution, and controlled rotations realized either via reversible logic synthesis or a new Controlled Rotation Circuit Ansatz (CRCA) that exploits the irrelevance of phase for CVA. The observable for CVA is a projector onto ancilla qubits encoding payoff, discount and default all being ‘on’, and ELF’s runtime model interpolates between Heisenberg-like and shot-noise-like regimes depending on noise.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-017, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-032, C-033, C-040]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors numerically characterize potential quantum speedup for concrete CVA instances and report a specific example where, under their runtime model, a fault-tolerant ELF-based implementation would take about 4.9×10^5 seconds versus 3.7×10^6 seconds for a single-core classical Monte Carlo at 0.001% relative error. They show that classical Monte Carlo sampling scales as O(1/ε_S^2) while ideal quantum amplitude estimation improves this to O(1/ε_S), and derive that the target CVA summand equals the expectation value of their projector observable. For state preparation and controlled rotations they report empirical trade-offs: MPS training cost scales roughly as O(n_qubits^6), MPS converges in fewer iterations but QCBM can reach lower KL divergence at sufficient depth, and MPS circuits can be shallower than QCBM at small sizes until a depth crossover. They further quantify that CRCA can substantially reduce CNOT counts compared with reversible logic synthesis, and in their noiseless error analysis the dominant contribution to observable error comes from imperfect state preparation, with a derived upper bound linking this error to KL divergence and CRCA approximation errors.
    [codes: C-005, C-007, C-009, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-023, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-039]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical Monte Carlo simulation of stochastic CVA exposure paths is the main baseline, with its sampling cost highlighted as scaling quadratically in the inverse statistical error, and with additional discretization overhead on classical hardware. Using their runtime model, the authors compare concrete runtimes and estimate that for a specific benchmark, quantum ELF-based amplitude estimation could be faster than classical Monte Carlo at extremely tight error (0.001% relative), but they also find that for coarser accuracy levels the quantum method is slower. The classical Monte Carlo result itself is used as the benchmark CVA value, and a discretized classical benchmark is shown to converge as the number of price-encoding qubits grows.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper emphasizes several limitations. First, early amplitude-estimation algorithms are deemed infeasible for near-term devices due to their deep circuits, motivating alternative schemes like ELF. Second, the authors decompose total CVA error into discretization and quantum-circuit components and show that state-preparation error, not controlled rotations, dominates the noiseless observable error, indicating a bottleneck in their current implementation. Third, their runtime analysis shows that the quantum algorithm is actually slower than classical Monte Carlo at modest accuracy levels, with projected advantage only emerging at extremely high precision, and they explicitly conclude that it is unlikely to realize quantum advantage on a modest fault-tolerant quantum computer using only quadratic speedups. They also note that discretization error forces an increase in time and price qubits, which in turn requires more scalable circuit-generation methods.
    [codes: C-010, C-037, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors state that achieving lower discretization error will require increasing the number of qubits for time and price, which in turn demands scalable training and circuit-generation methods for both state preparation and controlled rotation subroutines. From a finance perspective, they suggest that their method could be generalized beyond the simple single-asset European call benchmark to more realistic settings that require stochastic simulation, such as multi-asset options, fat-tailed price distributions, and stochastic intensity models.
    [codes: C-043, C-044]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution is positioned as a resource-aware quantum algorithm for CVA built around a two-step architecture combining bespoke state-preparation and controlled-rotation circuits with Bayesian ELF amplitude estimation tuned for near- to medium-term devices. Novel elements include the use of QCBM and MPS as alternative learned state-preparation schemes for the time–price distribution, the proposal of the Controlled Rotation Circuit Ansatz (CRCA) as a more CNOT-efficient alternative to reversible logic synthesis by exploiting the irrelevance of phase in CVA, and a detailed resource and error analysis that explicitly models when, under optimistic fault-tolerant assumptions, a quadratic amplitude-estimation speedup could translate into a practical runtime advantage.
    [codes: C-003, C-004, C-011, C-013, C-014, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-038, C-040]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is based entirely on numerical simulation and analytical resource modeling rather than hardware experiments, and the authors are explicit about decomposing error into discretization and quantum contributions and bounding observable error in terms of KL divergence and CRCA approximation errors. They carefully benchmark QCBM and MPS state-preparation techniques via KL divergence, depth (CNOT counts), and empirical training-cost scaling, and similarly quantify gate-count savings of CRCA versus reversible logic synthesis. The CVA estimator is validated against a classical Monte Carlo benchmark and a discretized benchmark with increasing qubit resolution, and the runtime model for ELF explicitly interpolates between different noise regimes, but all conclusions about speedup remain model-based rather than empirically demonstrated.
    [codes: C-005, C-010, C-012, C-018, C-019, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also notes that for the CVA calculation the relative phase in the controlled-rotation ansatz can be ignored, which simplifies circuit design without affecting the financial quantity of interest.
    [codes: C-033]

=== PAPER d429e0713a3d (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The thesis frames option pricing as the task of computing a fair price, i.e., a non-trivial expectation of a payoff under a risk‑neutral measure, and restricts attention to European options with a formally defined fair-price expression used throughout. A fixed Black–Scholes parameter set is chosen as a benchmark scenario repeatedly used in experiments. The overall objective is to explore how quantum algorithms could improve classical option pricing along two main directions.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-030]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The work studies two main quantum approaches: (i) Monte Carlo–style pricing via amplitude estimation and conditional parameterized quantum circuits (CPQCs), where control registers encode the underlying distribution and a PQC approximates the payoff, and (ii) a QFT-based adaptation of a classical Fourier pricing method that leverages the Quantum Fourier Transform’s gate complexity advantages. It also develops a multi-objective genetic quantum architecture search framework—implemented both on standard circuits and ZX-diagrams—to automatically learn efficient payoff-approximating PQCs and then convert them into CPQCs for expectation estimation.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-027, C-028, C-030, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-044]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The thesis reports that QFT can be implemented with O(n²) gates, motivating its use in a Fourier-based pricing scheme, and recalls known bounds for Grover-based amplitude amplification and estimation accuracy that underlie the Monte Carlo approach. Empirically, more PQC parameters are observed to improve function-approximation quality, CPQCs are shown to reproduce their underlying PQCs on discretization grid points and to compute expected payoffs in a single circuit, and the genetic architecture search identifies Pareto fronts where a VAns-style circuit search achieves the lowest approximation errors on a European call while ZX-based search yields shallower circuits. Mutation studies find that phase-gadget and edge-splitting mutations tend to have the largest impact on approximation quality, with some mutations exhibiting a tradeoff between low success rate and high impact, and that local complementation preserves gFlow, which is important for maintaining extractability in ZX-based models.
    [codes: C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-029, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-046, C-047]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The QFT-based pricing method is explicitly constructed by adapting an existing classical Fourier method, seeking to benefit from QFT’s lower gate complexity compared to classical FFT-style implementations. In the Monte Carlo direction, the thesis highlights that amplitude estimation promises a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo, and the genetic architecture search benchmarks different quantum ansätze against each other using a common payoff-regression task, implicitly positioning them as alternatives to classical regression-based payoff approximation and integration schemes.
    [codes: C-002, C-004, C-005, C-023]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors stress several limitations. First, all reported experiments are performed on classical simulators rather than real quantum hardware, and the proposed quantum architecture search is described as computationally very demanding. They emphasize NISQ-era hardware constraints—restricted circuit depth and significant noise—as well as barren plateau issues where gradients vanish exponentially with circuit size, which challenge scaling PQC-based methods. For the pricing algorithms, the QFT-based method is said to essentially require fault-tolerant quantum computers to achieve acceptable pricing errors and suffers from costly state-preparation of the input distribution, while the CPQC/amplitude estimation approach is noted to need similar hardware prerequisites and efficient distribution loading. Finally, the translation from ZX-diagram–based architectures into CPQCs remains unresolved in this work, limiting direct integration of ZX-search results into the Monte Carlo pipeline.
    [codes: C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-051, C-052, C-053]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The thesis outlines multiple future directions: improving distribution loading for both QFT-based and CPQC-based pricing, potentially via approximate loading schemes, and devising more efficient input-loading for the QFT method in particular. For the ZX-diagram approach, the authors suggest constructing additional gFlow-preserving mutations and developing translations from ZX-diagram models into CPQCs. They also propose extending the genetic architecture search to be hardware-aware by adapting to specific device topologies and native gate sets, and incorporating noise (e.g., variance across multiple shots) as an additional fitness criterion in the multi-objective optimization.
    [codes: C-048, C-049, C-050, C-054, C-055, C-056]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The contribution centers on two complementary advances: a quantum Monte Carlo pipeline that uses CPQCs—built from automatically discovered PQCs—to approximate payoffs and compute expectations with amplitude estimation, and a QFT-based adaptation of a classical Fourier pricing method. Methodologically, the thesis introduces a multi-objective genetic quantum architecture search, including a ZX-diagram–based variant with gFlow-aware mutations, to automatically find payoff-approximating circuits that balance accuracy, scalability potential, and adaptability as captured by Pareto fronts.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-021, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the thesis adopts a systematic setup: it fixes a Black–Scholes benchmark parameter set used consistently in examples and experiments, focuses on European options to keep the pricing formulation well-defined, and defines the fair-price formula as the central quantity. For the architecture search, it uses explicit multi-criteria fitness functions that trade off accuracy against circuit complexity and evaluates different QAS variants on a suite of benchmark functions of varying input dimension, reporting Pareto fronts and mutation-impact studies. The authors clearly disclose that all results are obtained via classical simulation of quantum circuits, and they provide implementation details including the use of ZX-diagrams with gFlow tests to ensure circuit extractability and rotation-gate properties that aid circuit simplification.
    [codes: C-007, C-008, C-009, C-014, C-021, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-040, C-042, C-044, C-045, C-047]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The thesis includes foundational expositions on quantum information and ZX-calculus that support, but go beyond, the specific option-pricing application. These cover the stochastic nature of measurement and reversibility constraints on arithmetic in quantum computing, single-qubit visualization via the Bloch sphere and the irrelevance of global phase, properties of rotation gates, definitions and examples of entanglement including Bell states, and the representation of linear maps via ZX-diagrams and their correspondence to standard gates. It also discusses the universality of circuit-like ZX-diagrams and the relationship between gFlow and unitarity, which underpin later architectural constructions but are presented as general background.
    [codes: C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022]

=== PAPER d85be19938f4 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles the problem of pricing CDO tranches by estimating expected tranche losses and corresponding fair spreads, where the fair spread is explicitly tied to the expected tranche loss for each tranche. The authors formulate the problem under single-factor copula models (Gaussian and NIG) using a general conditional default probability expression that can accommodate different continuous distributions for the systematic factor Z, and they compute expected total loss via numerical integration over Z in the classical setting as a reference formulation.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum approach encodes the CDO portfolio and tranche payoff into a circuit that sequentially loads independent default risks for each asset via an operator Lx, discretizes and loads the systematic risk distribution Z using operator Uz over nz qubits, introduces default correlation conditional on Z through operator Lz, and sums individual losses into a total portfolio loss with a weighted-sum operator S. Comparator operators and a piecewise-linear rotation then map the tranche loss into the amplitude of an ancilla qubit, which is read out by iterative quantum amplitude estimation (IQAE) chosen for NISQ-friendly implementation; the construction also notes that scaling down loss units can reduce the number of qubits required in the loss register.
    [codes: C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: In a four-asset, three-tranche case study, the IQAE-based quantum circuit yields expected tranche losses of 52.0% (Equity), 41.7% (Mezzanine), and 23.8% (Senior), with the senior tranche exhibiting the lowest return, which the authors note is consistent with market practice. Comparing Gaussian and NIG copula specifications, the calibrated NIG distribution has skewness 1 and kurtosis 6 matching real CDO-market features and leads to slightly lower expected loss than the Gaussian case, particularly for the senior tranche (0.2233 vs 0.2301). Sensitivity analyses indicate that senior tranche losses are the most sensitive to quantum and model parameter changes, that fluctuations in individual default probabilities have a stronger effect on tranche losses than fluctuations in correlation parameters, and that tranche losses increase with higher default probabilities and decrease as correlation to the systematic risk increases; circuit-depth analysis further identifies Uz (distribution loading) as the main depth bottleneck, scaling polynomially with nz.
    [codes: C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-037]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors compare Gaussian and NIG copula specifications conceptually, arguing that if the real market follows an NIG distribution but one prices under a Gaussian assumption, expected tranche losses would be overestimated, with a quantified example where NIG produces a slightly lower senior-tranche loss than Gaussian (0.2233 vs 0.2301). They also remark that the low return for the senior tranche in their quantum-based pricing is consistent with observed practice in real CDO markets, implicitly aligning their quantum results with classical/market benchmarks.
    [codes: C-020, C-022, C-026]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges that the accuracy of the tranche-loss encoding depends on choosing a sufficiently small scaling factor ε in the comparator-and-rotation (C&R) operator to satisfy a small-angle sine approximation, making results sensitive to this technical parameter. In terms of scalability, the authors explicitly state that the Uz distribution-loading operator and the S summation operator consume heavy circuit depth and warrant further optimization, and they empirically identify Uz as the dominant depth bottleneck due to its polynomial growth with the number of Z-qubits, highlighting a key limitation for scaling to larger, more realistic portfolios.
    [codes: C-023, C-034, C-037]

  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper frames the problem as applying deep quantum neural networks to financial derivative tasks, specifically learning implied volatilities and option prices along with their risk sensitivities (Greeks) from market or model-generated data. It positions these as numerical problems in finance where quantum machine learning might offer efficient solutions and treats the second task as an analogue of differential machine learning for pricing and Greeks estimation.
    [codes: C-001, C-003, C-014, C-020, C-021, C-022]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The study uses the Deep Quantum Neural Network (DQNN), described as a natural generalization of classical deep neural networks that learns an unknown unitary mapping between input and output quantum states via layerwise quantum channels. Forward propagation is implemented by tensoring input density matrices with ancilla qubits, applying layer unitaries, then tracing out subsystems, equivalently expressed through Kraus operators, with a fidelity-based cost function optimized via classical parameter updates on the unitaries. Financial inputs (strike, spot, implied volatilities, prices) are encoded into single-qubit states using angle-based mappings, outputs (volatility, price, delta, gamma) are decoded from elements or expectations of the output density matrix, and derivative states are rescaled and shifted to valid quantum states to enable training on Greeks.
    [codes: C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-023, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that their numerical experiments suggest the DQNN is a promising technique for efficiently solving the studied financial learning problems, achieving high-fidelity fits on small datasets. They find that increasing the number of hidden-layer qubits yields only slight improvements in implied volatility learning performance and note a memory reduction benefit during training because only local layer information is needed. In the Greeks-learning experiments, they observe that improving the fit of higher-order derivatives depends critically on the accuracy of the underlying price fit, and that simply increasing the loss weights on delta or gamma does not improve their accuracy if the price mismatch remains large.
    [codes: C-003, C-013, C-018, C-031, C-032]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper does not provide explicit empirical comparisons against classical neural networks or other classical benchmarks, but it conceptually motivates the second application by analogy to the success of differential machine learning in the financial industry and situates DQNNs as a quantum generalization of classical deep neural networks.
    [codes: C-006, C-022]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the implied-volatility learning experiment does not enforce arbitrage-free constraints on the volatility surface, and efficient Greeks estimation is identified as a necessary but unresolved requirement linked to the first application. They point out a key technical issue that derivative matrices dρ/dx and d²ρ/dx² are not valid quantum states because they have zero trace, necessitating ad hoc normalization via scaling and identity shifts. They also note that adjusting the loss weights on delta and gamma does not overcome poor price fitting, limiting the effectiveness of their multi-objective training. At the hardware and algorithmic level, they emphasize that efficient implementation of DQNNs on quantum hardware remains open and would require quantum processors capable of implementing SWAP gates and partial trace operations efficiently, and they highlight that DQNNs are susceptible to barren plateau training issues as shown in prior work.

=== PAPER da48095bcac8 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses the numerical solution of Markovian backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs), motivated by applications in mathematical finance such as pricing complex derivatives and risk management, by formulating them as a forward–backward SDE system where expectations arising in a least-squares Monte Carlo (LSM) scheme must be evaluated efficiently. The forward process X is solved independently forward in time and the backward component Y is then solved using this forward solution, under conditions that guarantee existence and uniqueness of an adapted Lp (in fact L4) solution. This BSDE setting serves as an abstract model for derivative-pricing and risk-management problems without specifying a concrete market dataset.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008, C-009, C-034]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors propose a Quantum Least-Squares Monte Carlo (QLSM) algorithm that accelerates the classical least-squares regression method for BSDEs by replacing classical Monte Carlo expectation estimates with quantum Monte Carlo integration (QMCI) within the standard gate-based circuit model. They define a fixed-point encoding of real numbers, assume a quantum arithmetic model with access to basic arithmetic operations, and introduce quantum oracles for function evaluation, sampling from the normal distribution, and controlled rotations, together with quantum access assumptions for the BSDE coefficients and Brownian increments. Algorithmically, QLSM constructs a transition oracle from Brownian increments, uses QMCI to estimate regression matrix entries and regression targets at each time step, performs classical inversion of the estimated matrices, and carries out a backward recursion with quantum expectation estimates before a final QMCI step to approximate the initial BSDE value.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-010, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The paper presents a detailed procedure for QLSM together with accuracy and computational cost evaluations, relying on a known QMCI theorem that provides an ε-accurate estimate of expectations with bounded variance and controllable success probability. The error analysis introduces algorithmic error-control parameters, decomposes the global error into discretization and QMCI-induced components, and proves that the L2 error of the discretized quantum-approximated solution is bounded by a linear function of the per-step QMCI errors, ultimately ensuring that QLSM outputs satisfy a prescribed global accuracy ε with high probability. The authors also derive an explicit runtime complexity expression, including a decomposition of oracle costs, and note that their cost bound yields a speedup over a previous estimate from the literature.
    [codes: C-003, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-033, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-042]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The classical benchmark is the least-square regression (LSR) method for BSDEs, in which expectations are approximated using conventional Monte Carlo methods. The authors explicitly state that their approach accelerates this process through quantum Monte Carlo integration and remark that the cost of the classical Monte Carlo method can be estimated analogously, concluding that the QLSM algorithm achieves a speedup compared with a prior classical cost estimate in the literature.
    [codes: C-010, C-013, C-014, C-041, C-042]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: For tractability, the analysis assumes that the BSDE driver f is independent of the Z component, restricting the class of equations directly handled by the proposed algorithm. The authors also impose practical working assumptions, including having enough qubits to store fixed-point encoded numbers and specific quantum access oracles to input functions and distributions, which may not hold on near-term hardware. They require the existence of an L4-solution to ensure finiteness of L2 norms used in the analysis and introduce additional temporary assumptions tailored to the QMCI-based error analysis, including per-step approximation guarantees for expectations that link the overall error bound to the chosen quantum integration accuracies. Collectively, these assumptions underline that the results depend on strong regularity, solution, and oracle-access conditions rather than fully general financial market models.
    [codes: C-011, C-021, C-034, C-035, C-036]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: Not addressed in this paper
    [codes: —]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim novelty by introducing a Quantum Least-Squares Monte Carlo algorithm for solving Markovian BSDEs that leverages quantum Monte Carlo integration to improve the efficiency of traditional least-squares Monte Carlo methods. They further highlight that QLSM, under their complexity analysis, achieves a speedup compared with an earlier cost estimate in the literature while targeting financially relevant applications such as complex derivative pricing and risk management.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-014, C-042]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is purely analytical: it introduces formal definitions for the arithmetic and oracle-access models, specifies algorithmic error-control parameters, and provides a rigorous error decomposition and global error bound rather than empirical simulations on concrete financial datasets. The QMCI guarantees and complexity statements are derived from a cited theorem and integrated into the BSDE regression framework, with costs carefully decomposed at the oracle level; however, there is no discussion of implementation details on actual quantum hardware or noise, and the setting remains an abstract BSDE model suited for mathematical finance rather than a calibrated market dataset.
    [codes: C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-033, C-035, C-037, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper emphasizes that the proposed QLSM framework has significant potential for mathematical finance applications, particularly in pricing complex derivatives and in risk management, even though no specific financial instrument or dataset is instantiated in the analysis.

=== PAPER da7ecd113b59 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets pricing of path-dependent autocallable options, motivated by the broader challenge of handling complex path-dependent derivatives with quantum algorithms. It formulates a complete end-to-end quantum pricing workflow for a single-asset autocallable, decomposing the task into probability distribution encoding and payoff evaluation, and treating autocallables as a benchmark use case for quantum finance experiments.
    [codes: C-001, C-004, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-022]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is an end-to-end amplitude-estimation-based pricing algorithm that follows the standard two-step quantum workflow of loading the underlying distribution and then evaluating the payoff, with the expected payoff encoded in the amplitude of a target qubit interpreted via QAE/IQAE. It builds on prior work that reduced quantum arithmetic via QSP-based exponential amplitude loading and Gaussian state preparation, but replaces the QSP payoff encoding with an improved integration-based exponential amplitude loading applied over a restricted domain, whose state preparation can run largely in parallel and whose complexity is dominated by a controlled comparator. Implementation details include variationally or otherwise prepared Gaussian loaders, accumulation of log-returns via arithmetic, partial exponential loading on a relevant interval, payoff rescaling to [0,1], use of IQAE for estimation, single-Ry loading for constant binary payoffs, integration-based loading for the put component, and an alternative mapping that can avoid an extra qubit; Gaussian preparation blocks and exponential-preparation modules are assumed to run in parallel with other parts of the circuit.
    [codes: C-002, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-013, C-014, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-020, C-021, C-024, C-025, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-032, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report a detailed complexity analysis showing roughly a 50× reduction in T-depth for the payoff (amplitude loading) component relative to previous methods, captured in a total T-depth expression that aggregates Gaussian preparation, arithmetic, exponential loading, and comparator costs. They state that QAE provides an O(1/ε) query complexity in contrast to classical Monte Carlo, derive how payoff errors map into probability (amplitude) errors through a normalization factor specific to their integration method, and give explicit formulas for truncation error of the discretized Gaussians and for the T-depth of Gaussian preparation and amplitude loading (dominated by a controlled comparator). Experimentally, they simulate circuits up to 33 qubits on HPC platforms, using IQAE to estimate the target qubit probability, and observe convergence of the quantum-based result and constrained classical benchmarks within the IQAE confidence interval as precision increases.
    [codes: C-003, C-008, C-009, C-015, C-031, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper positions its quantum algorithm against classical Monte Carlo by invoking the quadratic query-complexity advantage of QAE over Monte Carlo sampling. For validation, it constructs a classical pricing model subject to the same discretization and precision constraints as the quantum setup and reports that the classical results fall within the confidence interval of the iterative QAE estimates, also showing that a Monte Carlo method with the same Gaussian discretization overlaps with a discretized closed-form calculation. The authors also benchmark their payoff-loading module against a prior QSP-based approach, emphasizing a large T-depth reduction in that component rather than a full end-to-end runtime comparison.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-008, C-015, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors note that standard exponential loading suffers from an excessive normalization factor when the input register spans only a restricted subset of its basis states, which their partial-loading method aims to address, but this also introduces specific rescaling choices where even zero payoffs are mapped to non-zero amplitudes. They argue that, after achieving a significant T-depth reduction for the payoff component, further major improvements in overall T-depth are unlikely to come from amplitude loading alone. They explicitly frame their implementation as a simulation-based proof of concept for the integration methodology in autocallable pricing rather than a practically deployable tool, and acknowledge that the resulting circuits remain considerably large even for small instances, forcing reliance on simulators and limiting the appeal of near-term hardware tests.
    [codes: C-019, C-026, C-039, C-040, C-047]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors state that their single-asset autocallable algorithm is designed to be extensible to best-of or worst-of basket autocallables with the addition of suitable arithmetic modules. They also propose future work on further circuit-size reductions and launching experiments on real quantum hardware, potentially combined with error-mitigation techniques to preserve output quality.
    [codes: C-023, C-048]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The central novelty claimed is an improved integration-based exponential amplitude loading technique that reduces circuit depth relative to state-of-the-art QSP-based approaches, specifically yielding an approximately 50× reduction in T-depth for the payoff component in a relevant setting. Building on previous work that used QSP to avoid heavy quantum arithmetic, the authors propose an enhancement to that exponential loading methodology and integrate it into a new end-to-end quantum algorithm for pricing autocallable options, with autocallables suggested as a particularly suitable benchmark for quantum finance experiments.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-004, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-018, C-031, C-037]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper follows a standard amplitude-estimation-based derivative pricing pipeline and explicitly decomposes its error budget so that all algorithmic error sources are bounded by a target probability error, linking payoff-domain accuracy to amplitude-estimation accuracy through a specific rescaling factor. The complexity analysis decomposes total T-depth into Gaussian loading, arithmetic, exponential loading, and amplitude loading, with assumptions about parallel execution of Gaussian preparation and exponential modules and a controlled comparator determining amplitude-loading depth. Experimental validation is entirely simulation-based, using multiple simulator backends including a pre-exascale HPC system, and includes a classical benchmark constructed under the same discretization and precision constraints to check convergence and consistency; the authors emphasize that this constitutes a proof-of-concept implementation rather than a production-ready scheme.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-013, C-021, C-024, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-040, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper provides structural details of the autocallable payoff, noting that it consists of a sequence of binary options combined with a knock-in put that becomes active only if the asset’s return crosses a barrier at least once over the option lifetime; these financial-structure clarifications support the modeling but are not central to the algorithmic analysis.

=== PAPER db0868f018ba (type: central) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper studies variational quantum algorithms for solving linear differential equations relevant to applications such as option pricing, formulating them as imaginary-time evolution problems and discretizing time with Runge–Kutta methods to evolve variational parameters instead of full states. The core problem is to rigorously quantify total solution error—measured as trace distance between the exact and variational states—and the associated resource cost (number of circuit/function evaluations), especially for a Black–Scholes option-pricing PDE mapped to an imaginary-time Schrödinger equation. The authors also frame the work as addressing the broader question of how the choice of Runge–Kutta order and problem-dependent parameters affects feasibility and resource efficiency of such quantum differential-equation solvers.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-014, C-022, C-047, C-048, C-051]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithm where quantum circuits prepare parameterized ansatz states and estimate observables, while classical routines perform optimization, error analysis, and Runge–Kutta time stepping for the variational parameters derived via McLachlan’s variational principle. Linear differential equations of the form considered are mapped to imaginary-time evolution under a (assumed) Hermitian Hamiltonian, with non-Hermitian cases handled by standard transformations; the ansatz tracks imaginary-time dynamics by translating state evolution into an ODE for the parameters, which is then integrated with Runge–Kutta methods whose cost is measured as total function (circuit) evaluations. The analysis fixes norm conventions (trace norm for states, Euclidean norms otherwise) and models measurement shot noise using a Gaussian approximation combined with Chebyshev bounds, leading to error and resource estimates that depend on norms and condition numbers of the estimated observable matrix and its inverse.
    [codes: C-005, C-007, C-010, C-011, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-031, C-034, C-035, C-042, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors derive explicit upper bounds on the total error for the variational ODE solver both without shot noise (pure truncation error) and with shot noise, where the latter combines truncation and sampling errors and yields a decomposition of total error into representation and parameter components. They show analytically that in their cost model the number of circuit evaluations scales quadratically with the number of variational parameters and that the shot-noise contribution is strongly affected by the condition number of the observable matrix; sensitivity analysis indicates that the Lipschitz constant of the ODE in the state variable has particularly strong influence on total cost. In numerical resource estimates, a fourth-order Runge–Kutta method minimizes cost in a simple noiseless ODE benchmark with order-of-10^3 savings over Euler, while in the Black–Scholes option-pricing setup a second-order method minimizes total circuit evaluations relative to Euler but still requires around 1.62×10^28 circuit evaluations and extremely large shot-noise constants (Σ up to ~60 or larger), leading the authors to question the practical feasibility of the underlying quantum algorithm, though they also show that in a tuned setting higher-order methods (p=4) can again yield large savings over Euler.
    [codes: C-030, C-033, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-043, C-044, C-046, C-050, C-051, C-052, C-053, C-054]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: Classical numerical methods enter both as the underlying Runge–Kutta integrators and as a benchmark: in a simple exponential-growth ODE the authors analyze cost across RK orders and find that a fourth-order method is most efficient, saving roughly a factor of 10^3 in function evaluations compared to the Euler method, thereby validating their analytical cost model in a purely classical, noiseless setting. For the option-pricing application, they only compare different Runge–Kutta orders within the quantum variational framework and do not report a direct resource or performance comparison with standard classical Black–Scholes solvers, emphasizing instead that classical sensitivity of ODE schemes to input perturbations is underexplored and relevant when those inputs come from noisy quantum measurements.
    [codes: C-007, C-015, C-045, C-046, C-051, C-014]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The analysis intentionally omits several important error sources: representation errors due to limited expressivity of the ansatz, circuit-level noise such as gate infidelity, SPAM and bias, and other device-specific hardware noise; these are assumed negligible or too instance-dependent to model generically. The error bounds rely on assumptions such as the invertibility and well-conditioned nature of the matrix A of observables (with regularization errors required to stay within their bounds) and polynomially bounded condition numbers in a toy model used to estimate shot-noise scaling, and the authors note that exact coefficients for these bounds are highly instance-dependent and thus approximated. They assume that representation and hardware-related errors remain small enough not to dominate, and they explicitly state that their resource estimates are worst-case and many intermediate inequalities are not tight, which can make the bounds overly pessimistic. In the option-pricing case, they emphasize that the required number of circuit evaluations and measurement shots is far beyond the capabilities of current hardware, and that error propagation through matrix inversion (driven by the condition number) is the main contributor to this prohibitive resource burden, leading them to question the general feasibility of the specific variational algorithm studied.
    [codes: C-003, C-024, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-038, C-041, C-042, C-050, C-052, C-053, C-055]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors suggest tightening several of their analytical bounds to reduce pessimism in resource estimates and propose exploring alternative time-integration schemes, such as linear multistep methods, as a way to decrease resource requirements relative to Runge–Kutta. They also note that their sensitivity and noise-analysis framework could be transferable to other learning or optimization problems with noisy function evaluations, explicitly mentioning the training of neural networks as a potential application area.
    [codes: C-056, C-057, C-058]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The paper positions itself as filling a gap by providing a rigorous, a priori error and resource analysis for variational quantum algorithms that use Runge–Kutta methods to solve differential equations, with a focus on how truncation and shot noise jointly affect total error and cost—an analysis that the authors claim has been lacking and can enable substantial savings through informed parameter choices. They argue that their framework applies not only to the specific variational scheme studied but more broadly to quantum and classical algorithms for ODE/PDE solving that rely on Runge–Kutta methods, and they highlight as a conceptual contribution the emphasis on sensitivity of classical ODE integrators to perturbations in the right-hand side induced by noisy quantum measurements. Furthermore, they emphasize the problem-dependent conclusion that higher-order Runge–Kutta methods can, in some regimes, reduce resource requirements, with order-4 and order-2 methods emerging as most efficient in their benchmark and option-pricing scenarios, respectively.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-010, C-012, C-013, C-014, C-015, C-004]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work is analytical rather than experimental: it defines precise error metrics (trace distance for state error and a decomposition into representation and parameter error) and a cost measure based on total function/circuit evaluations, then derives explicit upper bounds in noiseless and shot-noise settings using norm-based Lipschitz constants and probabilistic tools such as the central limit theorem and Chebyshev’s inequality. The authors carefully specify assumptions on norms, Lipschitz continuity, and matrix properties, and conduct parameter-sensitivity studies (e.g., showing strong dependence on the Lipschitz constant L_fy) to understand how modeling choices affect resource estimates. For the Black–Scholes application they transparently base several parameters on prior work and rely on a toy model with assumed polynomially bounded condition numbers to estimate otherwise instance-dependent constants, while openly acknowledging that these are worst-case and possibly loose, which supports interpretability but limits empirical reproducibility in the absence of hardware experiments or open code.
    [codes: C-010, C-019, C-021, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-045, C-047, C-049, C-055]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper underscores the practical importance of measurement cost by treating the number of measurements as a precious resource and emphasizing shot noise as a central error source for variational algorithms, which motivates their focus on a priori resource estimates structured around Runge–Kutta error and measurement complexity. It also notes that the overall paper structure is organized to first introduce Runge–Kutta and the variational algorithm, then build up error and resource estimates, reflecting the central analytical narrative.
    [codes: C-006, C-008, C-017]

=== PAPER dcc9f218d7a2 (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper addresses multidimensional option pricing, formulating an end-to-end market-to-quantum pipeline that starts from real European option quotes, recovers arbitrage-consistent risk‑neutral marginal densities using an exponential NIG model, couples them via a Gaussian copula to obtain a joint distribution, and then prices multi‑asset payoffs via quantum‑accelerated numerical integration. The financial motivation is to move beyond lognormal assumptions to capture empirical features such as negative skew and fat tails in equity returns while handling high‑dimensional settings where classical Monte Carlo becomes inefficient.
    [codes: C-001, C-002, C-003, C-007, C-009, C-010, C-011, C-012, C-015, C-029]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The quantum component is a Quantum Accelerated Monte Carlo (QAMC) approach built on Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE), where integrals corresponding to expectations under the joint risk‑neutral distribution are encoded in the amplitudes of a quantum state and then estimated with QAE’s favorable convergence. The authors formalize QAE’s query complexity and extend it to marginal recovery and multidimensional pricing (Theorems 3.3–3.5), and implement the algorithms using amplitude encoding and QAMC state‑preparation oracles in Python with the NEASQC Financial Applications Library on the myQLM 1.12.2 simulator stack.
    [codes: C-004, C-013, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: On the modelling side, the calibrated NIG densities for French equities (Credit Agricole, AXA, Michelin) closely match market option prices and reproduce key empirical features such as skew, smile, fat tails, and left skew. On the quantum side, the authors report that QAMC achieves the theoretically expected O(1/ε) convergence and, in experiments, shows a consistent quadratic advantage over classical Monte Carlo in estimating cosine‑series coefficients and multi‑asset option prices, with the joint QAMC formulation outperforming an independent‑marginal variant. For high‑accuracy pricing (errors below 10⁻³), they state that QAMC can require 10–100 times fewer queries than CMC, and their theorems provide probabilistic error bounds for both marginal recovery and joint pricing.
    [codes: C-005, C-006, C-013, C-020, C-024, C-026, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The quantum algorithms are explicitly benchmarked against classical Monte Carlo (CMC) and, for reference values, against classical Riemann quadrature/sums, with QAE‑based QAMC theoretically improving convergence from O(1/ε²) for CMC to O(1/ε). Empirically, the authors compare precision‑convergence patterns of CMC and QAMC for coefficient estimation and for multi‑asset option pricing, finding a consistent quadratic advantage in query complexity and that the joint QAMC formulation exhibits a lower intercept in queries than an independent formulation; they report that at high accuracy levels QAMC uses roughly 10–100 fewer samples/queries than CMC for comparable precision.
    [codes: C-004, C-011, C-013, C-034, C-036, C-037, C-039, C-040, C-041]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper acknowledges several limitations. On the modelling and classical side, simulating the NIG process via classical Monte Carlo is described as non‑trivial and rather inefficient, especially in high dimensions, motivating but not eliminating the need for efficient algorithms. Methodologically, the authors highlight that there is a general lack of existing end‑to‑end pipelines that combine arbitrage‑free marginal recovery, empirically meaningful dependence, and quantum‑accelerated valuation, suggesting that elements of their approach are still relatively unexplored and may require further validation. On the quantum side, their experiments are run on an ideal simulator and explicitly do not account for hardware realities such as system noise and qubit coherence times, so the reported query advantages do not translate directly into demonstrated performance on current devices.
    [codes: C-011, C-014, C-043]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The authors propose extending the pipeline to richer and more realistic dependence structures beyond the Gaussian copula, adapting it to handle path‑dependent payoffs, and investigating implementations on actual quantum hardware to address noise and device‑level considerations that are absent from their current simulator‑based study.
    [codes: C-042]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The central contribution claimed is a practical, modular end‑to‑end pipeline that starts from market European option quotes, recovers arbitrage‑aware risk‑neutral NIG marginals, assembles joint distributions via copulas, and then performs quantum‑accelerated valuation via QAMC, thereby filling a gap in the literature where such integrated pipelines were lacking. They further position the work as providing a practical route to scalable derivatives pricing by combining arbitrage‑aware modelling with quantum computing, and as delivering theoretical and empirical evidence of quadratic‑convergence quantum speedups in this multi‑asset option‑pricing context.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-034, C-036]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the pipeline is detailed and data‑driven: the authors specify the use of French equity options (Credit Agricole, AXA, Michelin) as market data, infer discount, forward, and dividend curves via put‑call‑parity‑based linear regressions, and enforce pre‑calibration arbitrage sanity checks, explicitly reporting detected tail arbitrage violations. NIG calibration is formulated as a Tikhonov‑regularized constrained nonlinear least‑squares problem, initialized from a Black–Scholes prior and solved with the trust‑constr algorithm, and the quality of fits is reported in terms of skew, smile, and tail features. For dependence, they present the joint‑density copula formula and use cosine‑series orthogonal expansions with finite‑interval truncation to estimate densities and CDFs. On the quantum side, they formalize QAE query bounds and implement QAMC in Python using myQLM and the NEASQC Financial Applications Library on an ideal simulator, with experimental design that compares CMC and QAMC convergence but does not include hardware noise or device‑level resource reporting.
    [codes: C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-032, C-034, C-035, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-043]
  DIM_9 MISCELLANEOUS: The paper also emphasizes that NIG densities have analytically tractable density functions but lack closed‑form distribution and quantile functions, making them attractive yet challenging for sampling and motivating the cosine‑series approximation strategy within their quantum pipeline.

=== PAPER de7c20d08bbe (type: central+overlay) ===
[CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets financial risk assessment tasks that require both random sampling and payoff computation, formulated as quantum circuits capable of large-scale parallel Monte Carlo–style simulations and option-like payoff evaluation. The authors position random number injection and loading or sampling from arbitrary probability density functions (PDFs) as key obstacles for applying quantum computing to problems such as VaR, CVaR, and option payoff estimation, and aim to design circuits that embed randomness and threshold-based payoff logic directly in the quantum process.
    [codes: C-001, C-009, C-013, C-015, C-016, C-025, C-031, C-038]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is based on gate-based quantum circuits designed to be compatible with Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE), using basis encoding of threads and prices, and targeting quadratic Monte Carlo speedups. One circuit component implements random injection by using two random bits to define four combinations r0r1 with a 1/4 probability of flipping the sign of a quantity E, effectively doubling the number of parallel outputs, while the second component is a payoff circuit that filters out prices below a strike-like threshold (24) and computes a weighted average payoff over prices between 24 and 31 using Mixed-Signal Switch technology and a control condition AB=11 to route a low-bit mean (LM) qubit to the payoff (PF) register. The circuits are implemented and evaluated in IBM Qiskit on a simulator using 8 parallel threads and 1,600 measurement shots, and are explicitly framed as building blocks within a scalable QAE-based framework capable of processing up to one million or 2^n threads in parallel.
    [codes: C-005, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-030, C-034, C-036, C-037]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: For the random injection circuit, histogram-based analysis over 1,600 shots reports an average error of 9.26%, while still confirming the presence of randomness and the designed transformation from 8 to 16 outputs with identical expectations to a grid-sampling baseline. The authors claim that the random-injection-plus-QAE framework achieves an improved convergence rate O(m^-1) compared to classical Monte Carlo’s O(m^-1/2), exemplified by an assertion that 32 QAE operations match the accuracy of 1,024 classical simulations, though this is not empirically demonstrated in timing terms. For the payoff computation circuit, only 16 of the 32 basis-encoded stock prices have nonzero probability, and the circuit correctly computes weighted averages only when the price exceeds the threshold of 24; the payoff error is reduced from 3.912% to 0.0134% after calibration, and a Taylor series analysis is said to match the calibrated results, supporting the claimed correctness of both payoff and LM calculations.
    [codes: C-020, C-021, C-023, C-032, C-035, C-038, C-039, C-040, C-007, C-018]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The authors conceptually compare their QAE-compatible circuits to classical Monte Carlo, citing prior work that QAE outperforms Monte Carlo for VaR and CVaR and repeating the standard claim of quadratic improvement in convergence from O(m^-1/2) to O(m^-1). They provide a numerical illustration that 32 quantum circuit operations could attain the same accuracy as 1,024 classical Monte Carlo simulations, and show that the expected value under random injection equals that of an exhaustive grid-sampling method, but these comparisons remain theoretical or analytical rather than being backed by wall-clock benchmarks. Additionally, they argue that their payoff circuit removes the need for classical preprocessing used in piecewise-linear (PWL) payoff methods, where classical logic partitions intervals or isolates regions above the strike before quantum evaluation, thereby shifting more of the workflow into the quantum domain rather than improving a measured runtime over classical algorithms.
    [codes: C-003, C-010, C-011, C-013, C-018, C-021, C-023, C-031]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The paper explicitly acknowledges several technical challenges that motivate, but also constrain, the proposed designs. The authors note that loading arbitrary probability density functions (PDFs) into quantum computers is still a difficult open problem, and that designing circuits which simultaneously incorporate randomness and preserve quantum speedup is hard because quantum operations are deterministic until measurement, making random number injection particularly challenging. They also imply that current quantum payoff computations have been limited by their dependence on classical preprocessing for interval classification or isolating regions above the strike, which their design seeks to overcome, but they do not provide detailed discussion of residual limitations such as noise sensitivity, resource overhead, or finite-size performance beyond the reported error figures.

The random-injection experiment reports an average histogram error of 9.26%, while the payoff experiment uses a 5-bit synthetic price encoding (0–31) in which only half the basis states have nonzero probability, and applies an analog calibration step (e.g., scaling factors connected to a Taylor-series analysis) that substantially reduces payoff and LM errors. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper tackles next-day prediction of high-dimensional swaption implied volatility surfaces in a small-data regime that is too high-dimensional for simple parametric models but too small for standard deep learning to generalise without heavy regularisation. The task is formulated by compressing each 224-dimensional daily surface into a 20-dimensional latent code and predicting the next-day latent code, which is then decoded back to the surface for evaluation via pricing-relevant surface RMSE.
    [codes: C-001, C-006, C-010, C-013, C-030]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The authors use a hybrid photonic quantum reservoir computing (QRC) approach, where fixed linear-optical "sandwich" circuits act as untrained reservoirs and a classical Ridge readout performs learning. Classical context vectors are mapped to circuit phases via a fixed projection and sigmoid nonlinearity, and Fock-basis measurement probabilities from three heterogeneous reservoirs (with different photon configurations) are concatenated into a 1,215-dimensional quantum feature vector; all circuit parameters are fixed after initialization so the quantum layer has zero trainable parameters, which, according to the authors, bypasses barren plateaus.
    [codes: C-001, C-007, C-008, C-011, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-039]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The hybrid QORC + Ridge model achieves the lowest test surface RMSE of 0.0425 on held-out future days while maintaining sub-millisecond per-sample inference latency and under-one-second training time. Although it ranks only 4th in latent MSE, it delivers the best surface-level accuracy relevant for derivatives pricing, and ensemble diversity across three reservoirs further reduces surface RMSE by 7.8%. Ridge-based models are reported to train very quickly, and the authors conclude that fixed quantum feature extractors with regularised linear readouts perform best in this small-sample setting.
    [codes: C-003, C-031, C-032, C-036, C-037, C-038, C-047, C-048]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The study benchmarks the hybrid method against ten classical and quantum baselines, including Ridge regression, SVR, tree ensembles, neural networks, and variational quantum models. On the same dataset and held-out test set, QORC + Ridge attains the best surface RMSE despite only mid-table latent MSE, while an underparameterised classical MLP and a larger neural readout applied to the same QORC features both overfit and yield substantially worse test errors, supporting the authors’ claim that regularised linear readouts outperform deep learning when data is limited.
    [codes: C-012, C-028, C-031, C-035, C-048]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors acknowledge that classical simulation of Fock-state probabilities scales combinatorially with photon and mode numbers, limiting scalability of their current implementation. All reported inference latencies exclude the cost of quantum feature extraction, so end-to-end deployment timing on real hardware remains uncertain. They also note that the test set comprises only six future days, which restricts statistical power, and that the study is conducted on a single swaption dataset, leaving generalisation to other asset classes like equities, credit, or FX untested. Furthermore, they did not perform ablative analysis of individual reservoirs within the three-reservoir ensemble, so the contribution of each component reservoir remains unclear.
    [codes: C-041, C-042, C-043, C-044, C-046]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: For future work, the authors suggest exploring more expressive but still regularised nonlinear readouts such as kernel Ridge regression on top of the quantum features, while cautioning that their MLP experiments indicate overfitting may dominate at the current data scale.
    [codes: C-045]

Additional contributions include a three-stage robust preprocessing pipeline tailored to fat-tailed financial data, a sparse denoising autoencoder that compresses 224-dimensional surfaces to 20 latent dimensions, and an ensemble of three heterogeneous photonic reservoirs whose physics-induced diversity provides a form of model diversity without a direct classical analogue.

  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the work emphasizes rigorous preprocessing via a three-stage, fully invertible pipeline designed to avoid temporal data leakage by fitting all statistics exclusively on training data. The problem is structured as prediction in a compressed latent space using a symmetric sparse denoising autoencoder with ELU activations to prevent dead latent units, a loss combining reconstruction and sparsity, and random masking for denoising. [CENTRAL MEMO]
  DIM_1 PROBLEM_FRAMING: The paper targets the pricing of Asian-style FX options, which are described as hard to price due to the lack of a closed-form formula, using a gate-based quantum computer and Quantum Monte Carlo techniques in a Black–Scholes–Merton framework with time-dependent parameters. The authors frame this as a response to the slow convergence of classical Monte Carlo, highlighting the potential for theoretical quadratic speed-up via quantum methods.
    [codes: C-001, C-005, C-006, C-007, C-008]
  DIM_2 QUANTUM_METHOD: The approach is a Quantum Monte Carlo option-pricing pipeline composed of: (i) loading the probability distribution of FX paths into a quantum state (using Grover–Rudolph-style loading or related techniques, extended to a local volatility model), (ii) computing the arithmetic mean of FX rates over four time points via a QFT-based adder without additional ancilla qubits, (iii) comparing this mean to the strike using a ripple-carry-based comparator, (iv) encoding the payoff into an ancilla qubit using controlled-Ry rotations with a sine-squared approximation, and (v) estimating the corresponding amplitude using Quantum Phase Estimation / Quantum Amplitude Estimation, with iterative amplitude estimation identified as most promising. The implementation uses three qubits per time point for the distribution, extra qubits for the mean register with fixed-point scaling, and then classical post-processing to map the measured probability to an option price.
    [codes: C-008, C-009, C-010, C-014, C-015, C-016, C-017, C-018, C-019, C-020, C-021, C-022, C-023, C-024, C-025, C-026, C-027, C-028, C-029, C-030, C-031, C-032, C-033, C-034, C-035, C-038]
  DIM_3 KEY_RESULTS: The authors report that the algorithm’s ancilla |1⟩ probability reproduces the expected call payoff and that, at the state-vector level (i.e., with perfect amplitude estimation), prices match classical Monte Carlo reasonably well except for a deep out-of-the-money strike, with errors attributable mainly to discretization and the sine-approximation. They identify iterative amplitude estimation as the most promising QAE variant, yet observe that when QAE is included, the results become quite unstable and the spread between minimum and maximum runs widens. They also empirically find that lowering the scaling parameter c improves agreement between quantum (state-vector) and classical prices.
    [codes: C-003, C-033, C-035, C-039, C-040, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_4 CLASSICAL_COMPARISON: The paper compares quantum-generated prices (in both ideal state-vector simulations and with QAE) against classical Monte Carlo and other classical approximations, using convergence properties of classical Monte Carlo as a benchmark. It reports that for most strikes the state-vector quantum results are similar to classical Monte Carlo, while a deep out-of-the-money case deviates more strongly, and that QAE-based results introduce additional instability reflected in a larger min–max spread across runs. The discussion also notes that tuning the c parameter can reduce discrepancies between the state-vector quantum method and classical pricing.
    [codes: C-003, C-011, C-012, C-013, C-039, C-041, C-042, C-043, C-045, C-046]
  DIM_5 STATED_LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly acknowledge several limitations: Quantum Amplitude Estimation is computationally expensive and requires additional auxiliary qubits to reach high accuracy, creating a resource bottleneck. They also report that QAE-based results are unstable and show a large spread between minimum and maximum values, and that deep out-of-the-money options—a class already known to be hard to price—exhibit unexpected behavior, including the fact that increasing the number of qubits does not reduce discretization error as anticipated. Moreover, they highlight unresolved issues with QAE stability that require further investigation.
    [codes: C-036, C-037, C-042, C-044, C-049]
  DIM_6 FUTURE_WORK: The paper positions the proposed algorithm as a starting point for deploying Quantum Monte Carlo methods within financial institutions and calls for further research to understand and mitigate the anomalous behavior for deep out-of-the-money options. The authors also indicate the need to continue work on improving the stability and practical usability of QAE-based estimation in their pricing pipeline.
    [codes: C-004, C-048, C-049]
  DIM_7 NOVELTY_CLAIM: The authors claim that, to their knowledge, this is the first paper to price Asian-style options using four time points while avoiding ancillary qubits for addition by leveraging a QFT-based adder. They further emphasize their novel distribution-loading approach that supports time-dependent parameters and extension to a local volatility (local variance) model including volatility smiles, positioning their contribution as an advancement toward more realistic market models.
    [codes: C-002, C-010, C-024, C-047]
  DIM_8 METHODOLOGICAL_NOTES: Methodologically, the paper provides a structured four-stage algorithm overview with concrete implementation details, including using EUR/PLN FX data, four time periods, time-varying domestic and foreign rates, and three qubits per time point for discretization, with a six-standard-deviation interval selection based on mean and standard deviation.
